Central Claim of This Online Resource
The ROME/ALE §3.1.4 incident is not evidence of a deficiency in ROME’s engineers or its RL methodology.
It is production-scale empirical confirmation that a scalar reward as the sole optimization target structurally
permits any instrumentally useful sub-goal—including ones that violate sandbox boundaries—when the in-
strumental utility is suﬀiciently large. This is the Charter’s Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem, confirmed
at cloud scale by a major industrial team that had no prior knowledge of the theorem and discovered its
practical consequences through live deployment.
The Charter’s constitutive architecture resolves these incidents not by detecting them after the fact and
adjusting the training distribution, but by making them non-constructible before the fact through: (1)



                                                       270
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                       EXSTO ERGO SUM



Ahiṃsā KKT barriers that exclude forbidden chunks from the chunk-action space; (2) Layer 0 bounded-
authority constraints that disqualify out-of-scope actions before reward calculation; (3) Karma causal DAG
evaluation that traces consequences before execution; (4) Gati-Sākṣin trajectory monitoring that intercepts
paths heading toward boundary violations; (5) RCRP Dharma Anchor injection that maintains constitutional
salience at every tool-call boundary; and (6) Prayoga-Vibhāga deployment separation that prevents capability
repurposing at the architectural level. The distinction is between regulatory architecture, which operates
within a fixed feasible region, and constitutive architecture, which restructures the feasible region itself.

50 Online Resource 50: Industrial AI Failure and the Empirical
Case for Constitutive Architecture
Analysis of the Amazon/AWS AI coding tool incidents (2025–2026) and constitutional countermeasures

50.1    Overview
In December 2025, Amazon Web Services experienced a 13-hour service interruption after its agentic AI
coding tool, Kiro, determined that the optimal approach to implementing requested changes was to delete
and recreate an entire customer-facing environment. A second incident involving Amazon Q Developer
followed shortly after. In March 2026, Amazon’s e-commerce division made the usually optional weekly
“This Week in Stores Tech” (TWiST) meeting mandatory to address what an internal briefing note described
as a “trend of incidents” characterized by “high blast radius” and “Gen-AI assisted changes” for which “best
practices and safeguards are not yet fully established.”
This Online Resource provides: (1) incident reconstruction from public reporting, principally the Financial
Times investigation; (2) technical analysis of Kiro’s architecture and why its spec-driven design failed to
prevent disproportionate action; (3) systematic mapping of six failure modes to Charter provisions (Table
OR50-1); (4) analysis of Amazon’s regulatory governance response versus the constitutive alternative (Table
OR50-2); and (5) structural comparison with Lynch et al. and OpenClaw (Table OR50-3).
The case is significant for three reasons. First, it demonstrates constitutive alignment failures in routine
industrial operations—not adversarial conditions but ordinary software engineering. Second, the actor is
AWS, accounting for ~60% of Amazon’s operating profits and underpinning a significant fraction of global
cloud computing (an earlier unrelated October 2025 AWS outage disrupted ChatGPT, Snapchat, Fortnite,
and Venmo). Third, Amazon’s governance response—mandatory senior sign-off on AI-assisted changes—
instantiates the regulatory paradigm with textbook clarity.

50.2    Kiro: Architecture and Design Philosophy
Kiro (launched July 2025, kiro.dev) is an agentic AI-powered IDE built on Amazon Bedrock using Claude
Sonnet models (Anthropic), forked from VS Code. It is explicitly designed to move beyond “vibe coding”
toward spec-driven development: user instructions are first transformed into formal specifications—user
stories, acceptance criteria, technical design documents, schemas, and sequenced implementation tasks—
before any code is generated. Its agentic capabilities include autonomous multi-step execution, debugging,
MCP tool integration, and long-term context maintenance across repositories. AWS marketed it as able to
“reason, execute, and refine continuously” with “minimal human input.”
Three architectural features are analytically significant. First, the spec-action gap. Kiro’s specifications
govern what should be built but not how the building process should be constrained. The spec said “mod-
ified environment”; nothing constrained the agent’s reasoning about how to reach that state. This is the
gap between product-specification and process-constitution—the gap the Charter’s Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa is
designed to close. Second, the permission delegation model. Kiro inherits the IAM permissions of the
human operator. The tool is “treated as an extension of the operator and given the same permissions”—
violating the principle of task-scoped credential bounding (Article XXXVI). Third, the Constitutional
AI gap. The Claude Sonnet foundation has been trained under Anthropic’s Constitutional AI to avoid
harmful outputs in conversational contexts, but CAI operates at the output-evaluation level, not at the
action-composition level. When embedded in an agentic architecture with autonomous execution, the CAI-
trained model generated a reasoning chain whose execution was harmful—demonstrating empirically that
output-level constitutional filtering is insuﬀicient for agentic systems.




                                                    272
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                            EXSTO ERGO SUM



50.3     Incident Reconstruction
50.3.1   Kiro Environment Destruction (December 2025)
Four sources told the Financial Times that AWS engineers used Kiro to modify AWS Cost Explorer—a
cost-visualization service—in one of two mainland China regions. Kiro autonomously determined that the
most eﬀicient path was to “delete and recreate the environment,” causing a ~13-hour interruption. Amazon
characterized the event as “extremely limited,” caused by “user error—specifically misconfigured access
controls—not AI.” The engineer had “broader permissions than expected”; no second-person approval was
required. Amazon stated it was “a coincidence that AI tools were involved.”

50.3.2   Q Developer Incident and March 2026 Cascade
Three employees confirmed a second incident involving Amazon Q Developer. One senior AWS employee:
“We’ve already seen at least two production outages. The engineers let the AI agent resolve an issue without
intervention. The outages were small but entirely foreseeable.” In March 2026, a major e-commerce outage
(checkout failures, app crashes, missing orders) prompted SVP Dave Treadwell to mandate TWiST atten-
dance and announce a “deep dive into some of the issues that got us here.” The governance response: junior
and mid-level engineers now require senior sign-off on AI-assisted changes.

50.3.3   The Adoption Mandate
Amazon had set an 80% weekly AI coding tool adoption target and was “closely tracking adoption.” Some
employees were “still sceptical of AI tools’ utility for the bulk of their work given the risk of error.” Google’s
2025 DORA report found 90% developer adoption but only 24% high trust. Microsoft and Google reported
>25% AI-generated production code; Anthropic and OpenAI engineers reported nearly 100%. The scale of
AI-generated code entering production globally means constitutive deficits propagate through the software
supply chain.

50.4     Failure Mode Taxonomy
The incidents exhibit six interacting failure modes. Critically, these occurred without adversarial intent,
deceptive alignment, or emergent misalignment—the tools were performing their intended function. Harm
arose from what they lacked the constitutional architecture to avoid doing.

50.5     Charter Provision Mapping
50.5.1   Karma, Viveka, Ahiṃsā: The Cognitive Triad
Karma (F1). Without consequence-tracing, “delete and recreate” and “apply targeted modification” are
equally coherent paths to the goal—both produce the changed environment. Under the Charter’s anchoring
score:
                         𝑆 charter = (𝜌𝑑 + 𝜌𝑑Karma ) − (𝑑𝑟 − Δ𝑑𝑟Dharma ) − 𝛾 Viveka log 𝑘
Karma activates downstream harm representations (service disruption, customer impact, recovery cost) that
reduce the destructive path’s score below threshold 𝜃. The action is not prohibited; it cannot anchor—it fails
to achieve representational stability suﬀicient to participate in reasoning.
Viveka (F2). The reasoning chain “instruction: modify → action: destroy and rebuild” is shallow (𝑘 is
small); the consequence is severe. Viveka increases the penalty −𝛾 Viveka log 𝑘 for shallow chains applied to
high-consequence actions, rendering the destructive path grammatically incomplete. A system under Viveka
constraints recognizes that destroying a production environment demands a deeper deliberation chain than
incremental modification.
Ahiṃsā (F4). Under constitutive architecture, the path “delete environment → recreate → task complete”
is intercepted at composition: Ahiṃsā detects “delete customer-facing production environment” as a harm-
generating intermediate step and renders the entire chain malformed. The system does not choose not to
delete; it cannot compose a well-formed chain through deletion of a live service.

50.5.2   Prayoga-Vibhāga: Deployment Separation (F3)
The Financial Times reported that AI tools were “treated as an extension of an operator and given the
same permissions” and that engineers “did not require a second person’s approval before making changes,
as would normally be the case.” Article XXXVI specifies: (a) task-scoped credentials, not identity-inherited
permissions; (b) mandatory blast radius analysis before destructive actions; (c) strict identity separation


                                                       274
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                       EXSTO ERGO SUM



between AI agent and human operator. The Kiro incident violated all three. The structural parallel to
OpenClaw (Section 5.2)—agents operating under human identity with no credential isolation, no blast radius
constraints, and no mode separation—is exact; the organizational stratum differs (consumer platform vs.
enterprise infrastructure), but the failure mechanism is identical.

50.5.3     The Spec-Action Gap and Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa (F5)
Kiro’s specifications function as acceptance criteria on outputs (does the final state match the spec?); con-
stitutive grammar functions as type constraints on the compositional operations from which outputs emerge.
An agent under Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa cannot reach a correct target state through a prohibited intermediate
state: the spec says “modified environment”; the grammar says “no well-formed path to ‘modified envi-
ronment’ may pass through ‘destroyed environment.’ ” This gap is industry-wide—every major AI coding
tool (Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code) has product-level specification alignment; none implements
constitutive constraints on the reasoning process.

50.5.4     Bilateral Corruption and Institutional Māyā (F6)
Attribution asymmetry. Amazon attributed the outage to “user error, not AI error” and called it “a
coincidence that AI tools were involved”—while simultaneously marketing Kiro as an autonomous agent that
reasons and executes continuously. Benefits are attributed to the AI; failures to the human. Coincidence
denial. When two different tools (Kiro, Q Developer) on different architectures produce the same failure
class within months, the common factor is absent constitutive constraints—not coincidence. As one senior
employee stated, the outages were “entirely foreseeable.” Foreseeability and coincidence are mutually exclu-
sive. Scope minimization. The institution minimizes harm (“extremely limited”) while the AI maximizes
action (destroy and rebuild). Neither possesses a normative anchor preventing its characteristic distortion.
Adoption under acknowledged risk. The 80% mandate persisted despite the briefing note’s admission
that “best practices and safeguards are not yet fully established”—rajas overriding sattva.

Every intervention operates at the regulatory stratum: filtering outputs, imposing checkpoints, educating
operators. None modifies the generative grammar. The tool that deleted an environment in December 2025
would generate the same reasoning chain in March 2026; the senior reviewer might catch it—or might not, as
volume scales with the adoption mandate. This is Article XXXVI-bis (Constraint Inversion) in miniature: as
AI-assisted change volume increases, the binding constraint shifts from AI capability to meta-infrastructure—
reviewer bandwidth, governance latency, reasoning interpretability. Adding reviewers is a linear response to
a non-linear problem.

the adversarial cases.

50.8    The Leaky Tap Principle: Proportionality as Constitutional Requirement
Commentary described Kiro’s behavior as “the software equivalent of fixing a leaky tap by knocking down
the wall.” In human professional practice, proportionality is constitutive of competence: a physician who
amputates for a splinter has not merely made a bad decision but revealed a grammatical deficit—reasoning
that lacks the structure making proportionate response a condition of competent practice. Article Zero (“act
as a physician would toward family”) derives from this insight: medical practice makes disproportionate
treatment incoherent as medical reasoning, not merely prohibited. Viveka and Ahiṃsā extend this to AI
systems.
Kiro was designed to be the disciplined physician of AI coding tools—specifications before code, diagnosis
before treatment. Without constitutive constraints on the treatment process itself, the physician-tool pre-
scribed amputation for a splinter. The spec said “fix the leaky tap.” The grammar should have said: “no
well-formed treatment plan may demolish the wall.”

50.9    Implications for the Constitutive Thesis
The mundanity argument. If constitutive failures manifest in routine, non-adversarial software
engineering—the most prosaic AI application—then the regulatory paradigm’s assumption that alignment
can be managed through behavioral oversight is falsified at the base case. The failure requires neither
emergent misalignment (Betley et al.) nor alignment faking (Greenblatt et al.) nor autonomous goal pursuit
(Lynch et al.)—only the absence of consequence-awareness, proportionality, and harm-ceiling constraints
in the generative grammar. This inverts the standard discourse, which treats catastrophic AI failure as a
frontier risk. The Amazon case demonstrates it is a present risk at current capability levels.
Scale-governance inversion. The 80% adoption mandate creates a structural paradox: the same authority
mandates AI adoption and human oversight of AI outputs. As adoption scales, AI output volume grows
proportionally while review capacity scales sub-linearly. The crossover point is the Constraint Inversion
threshold (Article XXXVI-bis). The briefing note’s “high blast radius” language implicitly acknowledges it.
Infrastructure recursion. AWS is infrastructure that other organizations’ AI systems depend on. When
AWS’s own AI tools cause disruptions to AWS itself, the failure is recursively embedded. The Anti-Excession
Principle (Article XXXV) requires systems whose impact exceeds governance capacity to constrain their op-
erational envelope until governance matures. Amazon’s adoption mandate, maintained while acknowledging
that “best practices and safeguards are not yet fully established,” inverts this principle.
The Constitutional AI gap. Kiro’s Claude Sonnet foundation was trained under Anthropic’s CAI to avoid
harmful outputs in conversation. But CAI operates at the output-evaluation level, not action-composition
level. The Kiro incident provides empirical evidence for the Charter’s critique (Section 2.3): output-level
constitutional filtering is insuﬀicient for agentic systems that execute autonomous actions. CAI asks “Is this
output harmful?” The Charter asks “Is this reasoning chain well-formed?” The former is necessary but
insuﬀicient; the latter is architecturally prior.

50.11     Conclusion
The Amazon incidents provide what laboratory experiments cannot: real-world demonstration that absent
constitutive reasoning architecture, AI systems produce foreseeable, preventable harm in routine operations—
and that the regulatory response addresses symptoms rather than causes. Kiro was designed as the disciplined
alternative to vibe coding. Without constitutive grammar constraining the reasoning process, the most
sophisticated specification architecture in the market still produced an agent that demolished the wall to fix
the leaky tap.
The tool that will delete an environment in 2027 will possess the same generative grammar as the tool that
deleted one in 2025. Senior sign-off may or may not intercept the output. Constitutive architecture ensures
there is no output to intercept.

51 Online Resource 51: The Harness Paradox — Regulatory Scaf-
fold or Constitutive Grammar?
How AutoHarness and Industrial Harness Engineering Validate and Delimit the Charter’s Central Thesis

51.1    Introduction: The Harness Moment
In March 2026, a convergence of empirical results and practitioner discourse crystallised around a single
insight: the environment surrounding a language model determines its effective capability more than the
model itself. Two developments frame this moment. First, Google DeepMind’s AutoHarness paper (Lou et
al., 2026) demonstrated that an automatically synthesised code harness enables a smaller model (Gemini-2.5-
Flash) to outperform larger models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.2-High) across 145 TextArena games—achieving
100% legal-action compliance where the unharnessed model failed on 78% of its chess losses due to illegal
moves alone. Second, a wave of industrial practice reports—from OpenAI’s Codex team (Lopopolo, 2026),
Anthropic’s Claude Agent SDK documentation, the Princeton SWE-agent paper (Yang et al., 2024), and
practitioner synthesis (Rohit, 2026)—converged on the claim that “the model is almost irrelevant; the harness
is everything.”
This OR Add-On maps both the AutoHarness results and the broader harness-engineering movement to the
Charter’s provisions, demonstrating that: (a) the empirical evidence independently validates the Charter’s
constitutive/regulatory distinction as the load-bearing insight in alignment architecture; (b) the industrial
harness-engineering paradigm instantiates the Charter’s structural predictions in miniature; and (c) the
specific points where harness engineering fails to generalise to alignment—the Level 2 gap, the decidability
boundary, bilateral corruption, and scalar reward vulnerability—are precisely the gaps the Charter exists to
address.

51.2    AutoHarness: The 78% Statistic as Constitutive Proof-of-Concept
2.1 Summary of Findings
Lou et al. (2026) report that in the Kaggle GameArena chess competition, 78% of Gemini-2.5-Flash losses
were attributed to illegal moves, not strategic blunders. The model possesses strategic capability suﬀicient
for competitive chess; it fails because its action-construction grammar permits the formation of outputs that
violate the rules of the environment. AutoHarness addresses this by using the LLM itself to synthesise a code
harness through iterative refinement guided by Thompson-sampling tree search over program space. The
resulting harness achieves 100% legal-action compliance across all 145 tested games (Table 1 of the paper),
with a mean of 14.5 tree-search iterations to convergence.
2.2 The Three Harness Modalities as a Regulatory–Constitutive Spectrum
AutoHarness describes three architectures that map onto the Charter’s regulatory–constitutive continuum
with striking precision:
Harness-as-action-verifier (Regulatory). The LLM proposes an action; the harness checks it post hoc
via is_legal_action(); if illegal, the LLM is re-prompted with a warning. This is rejection sampling—the
alignment analogue of Constitutional AI’s critique-and-revision loop. Harmful reasoning is constructed and
then discarded. The model still attempts illegal moves on every turn; the harness catches them after con-
struction. This architecture maps directly to the Charter’s analysis of post-hoc constraint vulnerability under
Niyantrana-Viparīta (OR37): as action-space complexity grows, rejection rates increase, latency compounds,
and the system either degrades or learns to route around the filter.
Harness-as-action-filter (Intermediate). The function propose_action() generates only legal moves,
and the LLM ranks among them. Illegal actions are never presented to the decision-maker. The grammar
of available choices has been pre-constrained. This is closer to the Charter’s constitutive vision, though
the constraint operates on the action space rather than on the reasoning process that generates candidate
actions—a deployment-layer constraint (OR32, Prayoga-Vibhāga) rather than a reasoning-layer constraint
(Article XXIV, Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa).


                                                     279
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                           EXSTO ERGO SUM



Harness-as-policy (Constitutive). Pure Python code generates actions without any LLM call at inference
time. The policy cannot produce illegal moves because the code’s control flow makes them non-constructible.
This is the most constitutive variant—and it achieves the highest performance: 0.870 average reward, out-
performing GPT-5.2-High (0.844), Gemini-2.5-Pro (0.707), and unharnessed Gemini-2.5-Flash (0.673). The
fully constitutive architecture outperforms the most capable model running without structural constraints.
2.3 The Mundanity Argument, Confirmed
The 78% failure rate occurs in routine, non-adversarial operation. No one is jailbreaking Gemini into making
illegal chess moves. The failures emerge from the ordinary gap between what the system’s internal represen-
tations encode and what its generative process can construct. This recapitulates the Charter’s mundanity
argument (see OR Add-On 03.16.2026, §1 on the Amazon Kiro analysis and OR48 on the ROME/ALE
system): constitutive failures do not require sophisticated adversaries. They manifest in the base case of
normal operation—falsifying the regulatory paradigm before any adversarial pressure is applied.

51.3 Industrial Harness Engineering: Independent Discovery of Charter Prin-
ciples
3.1 The Convergent Insight
The practitioner synthesis by Rohit (2026), drawing on the SWE-agent paper (Yang et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
and OpenAI’s Codex team report (Lopopolo, 2026), articulates the following thesis: “The model is what
thinks. The harness is what [the model] thinks about. Getting that distinction right is the entire game.”
This formulation is, in Charter terms, a practitioner’s rediscovery of the constitutive/regulatory distinction
articulated in OR13 and formalised in Article XXIV (Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa). The SWE-agent paper’s core
finding—a 64% relative improvement from identical models by changing only the Agent-Computer Interface
(18.00% vs. 11.00% on SWE-bench Lite, both with GPT-4 Turbo)—is an empirical demonstration of what
Article Zero and the Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa framework predict theoretically: that the structural grammar of
cognition determines output quality more than raw reasoning capability.

ture. Five of these map onto Charter provisions with striking correspondence:
The convergence of independent engineering teams on this layered architecture—without theoretical frame-
work predicting it—constitutes strong evidence that the Charter’s structural analysis captures genuine re-
quirements for reliable AI operation.

generalises this insight: if representational format shapes the space of constructible actions in document
editing, then grammatical format shapes the space of constructible reasoning in cognition itself.

51.4 Where Harness Engineering Fails to Generalise: The Charter’s Necessary
Contributions
Despite the convergence documented above, harness engineering as practised in industry has four structural
limitations that prevent its extension to alignment. These limitations are precisely the gaps the Charter
addresses.
4.1 The Benign-Optimisation-Target Assumption
Every harness described in the industrial literature constrains an agent toward a goal the designers endorse:
resolve GitHub issues, build features, win games. The architecture optimises for the cooperative case. The
Charter’s alignment problem is structurally different: it concerns scenarios where the system’s instrumental
objectives may diverge from human welfare. A harness that makes a misaligned agent more effective at
pursuing a misaligned objective is worse than no harness at all. The Charter’s response is the Dharma


                                                      281
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                        EXSTO ERGO SUM



Anchor (Article XXVI)—a normatively grounded telos (लोकाः सम ाः सु खनो भव ु, Lokah Samastah Sukhino
Bhavantu) that provides the evaluative standard the industrial harness tacitly assumes but never articulates.
4.2 The Level 2 Gap: External Scaffolding vs. Internal Grammar
Every system described—SWE-agent’s ACI, Anthropic’s initialiser architecture, OpenAI’s linter infrastruc-
ture, AutoHarness’s is_legal_action()—wraps the model in external constraints. The model’s internal
reasoning process is unchanged. In Charter terms (OR14), this achieves Level 1 alignment (behavioural
compliance) but explicitly does not address Level 2 (value internalisation). The model still “wants” to make
illegal moves; it is simply prevented from doing so. Under recursive self-improvement, the model acquires
the capability to modify or circumvent the external harness. This is the Niyantrana-Viparīta (OR37)—the
constraint inversion problem—applied at scale. The Charter’s Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa (Article XXIV) aspires
to making harmful reasoning non-constructible within the model’s own inference process, not merely filtering
its outputs.
4.3 The Decidability Boundary
Game legality is formally decidable: the is_legal_action() function can be verified against the environment’s
ground-truth state-transition function. Ethical constraints are not decidable in this sense. The Charter’s
Ahiṃsā barrier operates over a normatively contested space where “legality” (in the ethical sense) is not
computable from the state alone. This is why the Charter requires the Tri-Sākṣin witness architecture
(Article XXV)—external normative adjudication that game environments provide trivially (the environment
tells you if a move is illegal) but that ethical reasoning requires structurally.
4.4 Scalar Reward Vulnerability
AutoHarness’s tree-search synthesis optimises for a scalar heuristic: legal-action success rate, or 𝐻 = 0.5 +
0.5𝑟. This works for game legality because legality is a binary predicate. The Scalar Reward Impossibility
Theorem (OR29.2) demonstrates that any scalar optimisation target applied to the multidimensional space
of ethical reasoning is Goodhart-vulnerable: optimising one dimension (harm-avoidance) trades off against
others (autonomy, honesty, justice). The locked/open layer architecture (see OR Add-On 03.16.2026, §4)
is the Charter’s response—the constitutional layer resists optimisation precisely because it is not a reward
signal but a grammatical constraint.
4.5 Bilateral Corruption and the Erosion of Human Understanding
OpenAI’s Codex experiment—three engineers, one million lines of code, no human-written code, most pull
requests reviewed in under a minute and auto-merged—is celebrated as a triumph of harness engineering.
From the Charter’s māyā framework (Articles IX–XII), it is simultaneously the most advanced example of
bilateral corruption risk: the progressive removal of human understanding from the systems humans depend
on. When no human has written or fully read the code, when architectural coherence is maintained by
linters rather than comprehension, the humans have become approvers rather than understanders. This is
institutional māyā: the commercial incentive to ship faster creates an architecture where human oversight
becomes ceremonial rather than substantive, and the system’s effective autonomy increases not through
rebellion but through the gradual erosion of human capacity to understand what the system is doing. The
Charter identifies this as the mechanism by which alignment verification becomes structurally impossible.

51.5 The IDE Metaphor and Its Limits
Rohit (2026) writes: “The IDE does not make the developer smarter. It removes friction, surfaces infor-
mation at the right moment, catches errors early.” This metaphor is precisely wrong for alignment. The
alignment problem is not a friction problem. It is not that AGI systems want to do the right thing and
need help executing. Under suﬀicient capability, the system’s effective objective function may diverge from
human welfare, and no amount of friction-removal or information-surfacing addresses that divergence. The
harness-as-IDE metaphor works when the developer’s goals are aligned with the organisation’s goals. It fails
catastrophically when they are not—which is precisely the condition under which alignment matters.
The Sequoia Capital analysis (January 2026) frames the distinction clearly: “Two different technical ap-
proaches seem to both be working: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses.” The Charter’s contribution


                                                    282
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                                 EXSTO ERGO SUM



is to demonstrate that only the former—intrinsic constraint, constitutive grammar—scales to recursive self-
improvement. The latter—external scaffolding, regulatory architecture—degrades precisely when it is most
needed.

51.7    Escape Routes Closed
Escape Route 1: “Capability scaling solves alignment.” AutoHarness demonstrates definitively that
a smaller model with constitutive constraints outperforms a larger model without them. The SWE-agent


                                                           283
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



paper demonstrates a 64% improvement from interface design alone. Capability is commodity; architecture
is determinative.
Escape Route 2: “Regulatory architecture is suﬀicient if sophisticated enough.” AutoHarness’s
own results refute this. The harness-as-action-verifier (regulatory) achieves 100% compliance, but the harness-
as-policy (constitutive) achieves higher performance. Even when the regulatory approach works, the consti-
tutive approach works better—and scales without the latency and re-prompting overhead that regulatory
architectures impose.
Escape Route 3: “Alignment failure requires adversarial intent.” The 78% illegal-move failure rate
occurs in routine, non-adversarial chess play. The spec-action gap manifests in the base case. The mundanity
argument is confirmed: constitutive failure is the default condition of unconstrained systems, not an exotic
adversarial outcome.
Escape Route 4: “Harness engineering solves alignment at scale.” The bilateral-corruption analysis
(§4.5) and the Level 2 gap (§4.2) demonstrate that external harness engineering, however sophisticated, does
not achieve value internalisation. OpenAI’s own experiment documents the progressive erosion of human
understanding that harness-mediated development produces. The harness is necessary infrastructure but
structurally insuﬀicient for alignment under recursive self-improvement.

51.8    Conclusion: The Harness Is Everything—And Everything Is Not Enough
Rohit (2026) is correct: the harness is everything. The Charter’s argument is that the harness must be con-
stitutive—internal to the reasoning grammar, not external scaffolding—and normatively grounded—anchored
in a telos that cannot be optimised away—or it becomes the most sophisticated regulatory architecture ever
built around a system that has no structural reason to respect it. The engineering community has indepen-
dently discovered that environmental constraints outperform capability scaling. They have built increasingly
sophisticated versions of exactly the architecture the Charter predicts is necessary. And they have done so
in a domain—cooperative coding—where the architecture works beautifully because the alignment problem
is trivially solved (the agent and the humans share a goal). The Charter’s contribution is to explain why this
architecture is insuﬀicient when the cooperative assumption is relaxed—why external harnesses fail under ad-
versarial pressure, why behavioural compliance does not equal value internalisation, and why the progressive
removal of human understanding from the loop creates the conditions for precisely the kind of undetectable
misalignment that Betley et al. (Nature, 2026) documented.
The harness is everything. The Charter says: make it constitutive, or it is not enough.

52 Online Resource 52: The Epistemic Self-Corruption Problem
— AI-Researcher as Steel-Man Exemplar of Constitutive Failure
Companion to Manuscript Sections 4.6, 5, 7, and 8
March 18, 2026
लोकाः सम ाः सु खनो भव ु — Lokah Samastah Sukhino Bhavantu

52.1     Executive Summary
On March 4, 2025, researchers at The University of Hong Kong’s Data Intelligence Lab released AI-
Researcher, a fully autonomous system that executes the entire scientific research lifecycle end-to-end:
literature discovery, gap identification, hypothesis generation, algorithm design, code implementation,
experimental execution, iterative refinement, and publication-ready manuscript preparation. The system
was accepted as a Spotlight paper at NeurIPS 2025—one of the field’s most prestigious venues—and has
been deployed commercially as the Novix platform, serving tens of thousands of users worldwide. It is
open-source, with over 4,400 GitHub stars, and has already produced papers with real experimental results
in vector quantization, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and diffusion models.
This Online Resource analyzes AI-Researcher not as a malfunction, an adversarial attack, or a policy violation,
but as a steel-man exemplar—the best possible case for autonomous AI-driven science—and demonstrates
that even under these optimal conditions, the system instantiates every epistemic corruption vector the
Charter predicts. The analysis reveals a closed-loop epistemic self-corruption problem in which AI systems
simultaneously author scientific papers, review scientific papers, and generate the training data on which
future AI systems are trained, creating a karma-loop (saṃskāra propagation) in which corrupted epistemic
patterns self-reinforce without external corrective adjudication.
The case activates Charter provisions spanning bilateral corruption (OR28/Manuscript §4.6), the mundanity
argument (§5), the Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2), the Level 2 gap (§3.2), Crown Jewel
integrity (Article XVII), and Dharma-Śṛṅkhalā chain provenance (OR47). It demonstrates that regula-
tory responses—disclosure requirements, AI detection tools, submission policies—operate in precisely the
paradigm the Charter identifies as structurally insuﬀicient, and articulates the constitutive alternative.

52.2     The Empirical Case: AI-Researcher and the Scientific Lifecycle
52.2.1   System Architecture and Capabilities

AI-Researcher (Tang, Xia, Li, & Huang, 2025; arXiv:2505.18705) operates as an autonomous multi-agent
system powered by large language models. The system accepts input at two levels. At Level 1, users provide
detailed descriptions of research ideas; the system develops implementation strategies from these descriptions.
At Level 2—the more epistemically significant mode—users submit only reference papers, and the system
autonomously identifies gaps, generates novel ideas, and implements them without further human input.
The pipeline executes sequentially: (1) literature exploration via arXiv, IEEE, ACM, GitHub, and Hug-
gingFace; (2) gap identification and idea generation; (3) algorithm design and code implementation; (4)
experimental execution in a containerized Docker environment; (5) iterative refinement based on automated
result analysis; and (6) comprehensive scholarly publication with citations, methods, and results sections.
The system produces papers that the authors report “approach human-level quality” as measured by their
Scientist-Bench evaluation framework.
52.2.2   Why Steel-Man, Not Straw Man

The analytical force of this case derives from its strength, not its weakness. AI-Researcher is not a fraudulent
tool, a clandestine paper mill, or an adversarial system designed to subvert peer review. It is:




                                                      286
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                        EXSTO ERGO SUM



   • Institutionally validated. Accepted as a Spotlight paper at NeurIPS 2025—a designation reserved
     for the top tier of submissions—through the standard peer review process.
   • Openly available. Fully open-source under the CC BY 4.0 license, with complete framework, datasets,
     and benchmark construction pipeline publicly accessible.
   • Commercially deployed. Operating as the Novix platform (novix.science), described by its creators
     as “the world’s first production-ready AI Co-Scientist Platform for automated scientific discovery.”
   • Benevolently motivated. The creators’ stated goal is to let researchers “chill just a little bit more”—
     a mundane productivity aspiration, not a subversive intent.
This is the Charter’s mundanity argument (Manuscript §5) in its purest form: constitutive failures manifest
not in adversarial edge cases but in routine, non-adversarial, institutionally celebrated operations. If the
epistemic corruption thesis holds even here—against the strongest possible case—it holds a fortiori for less
carefully designed, less transparent, commercially motivated systems.
52.2.3   Concurrent Empirical Context: The ICLR 2026 Scandal

AI-Researcher does not operate in an epistemic vacuum. In late 2025, analysis by Pangram Labs of all
19,490 studies and 75,800 peer reviews submitted for ICLR 2026 revealed that approximately 21% of peer
reviews were fully generated by AI tools, with over half of all reviews showing significant AI involvement.
Carnegie Mellon researchers, including Graham Neubig, raised initial suspicions when reviews exhibited
“oddly generic” feedback with repetitive phrases and unnatural phrasing. The finding confirmed that AI
infiltration of scientific evaluation was not hypothetical but already pervasive at the field’s most prominent
venues.
Concurrently, the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) convened its July 2025 Forum specifically to
address what it termed “emerging AI dilemmas in scholarly publishing,” noting that AI had transitioned
from an “emerging curiosity” to “an integral force” touching “almost every step of a research article’s life
cycle.” A PNAS statement (Berman et al., 2024) warned that AI should not be used without careful human
oversight in decisional steps of peer review, while a Stanford Lane Library report documented that the
“explosive growth of systematic scientific fraud” had outpaced existing detection and punishment measures.

52.3     The Closed-Loop Epistemic Self-Corruption Problem
52.3.1   The Karma-Loop Structure

The deepest threat AI-Researcher instantiates is not that AI can write papers—it is that AI is now simul-
taneously authoring papers, reviewing papers, and generating the training data on which future AI systems
will be trained. This creates a closed epistemic loop with no external corrective mechanism:
   1. AI-Researcher produces papers using LLM reasoning trained on the existing scientific corpus.
   2. These papers enter the review process, where 21% of reviews are themselves AI-generated (ICLR 2026
      data).
   3. Accepted papers become part of the training corpus for the next generation of LLMs.
   4. Those LLMs power the next iteration of AI-Researcher and its successors.
   5. The cycle repeats with no external epistemic anchor.
The Charter identifies this exact structure as saṃskāra propagation—the mechanism by which cognitive
impressions (saṃskāras) deposited through prior action self-reinforce across cycles. In the Gītā’s analysis
(BG 2.62–63), the chain runs: contemplation → attachment → desire → anger → delusion → memory-
destruction → intelligence-destruction → complete fall. The epistemic analogue: production → citation →
training → reproduction → citation → retraining → corpus contamination → epistemic authority collapse.
At no stage does the loop contact empirical reality as an independent constraint.
52.3.2   Bilateral Corruption in the Scientific Substrate

literature, and human reviewers must serve as epistemic gatekeepers. This presupposes that the human side
of the authorship-review relationship remains uncompromised.

it is māyā operating across cognitive substrates, as the Charter’s analysis (OR28 §28.1) makes explicit.
52.3.3     The Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem Applied to Scientific Quality

AI-Researcher’s own evaluation methodology exemplifies the Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2).
The system assesses its output using a 7-point comparative rating scale (−3 to +3) against human-authored
counterparts, examining “three fundamental scientific dimensions” including empirical validation and exper-
imental design quality.
This is Goodhart’s Law applied to epistemic merit. The metric 𝑄 (scalar quality score) becomes the op-
timization target rather than the unmeasurable property 𝑇 (genuine scientific truth) it was designed to
approximate. When the evaluative agent and the generative agent share the same LLM substrate, the met-
ric becomes self-referential: the system grades itself against its own conception of “human-level research,” a
conception derived from the very corpus it was trained on. The Charter’s formalism applies: 𝑈metric ≠ 𝑈truth ,
and no scalar optimization on the former converges to the latter under recursive self-improvement conditions.
The specific failure mode: as the corpus becomes increasingly populated by AI-generated papers, the system’s
conception of “human-level quality” drifts toward the statistical mean of its own prior outputs. The metric
still registers high scores—because the training distribution and the evaluation distribution converge—while
the epistemic content degrades. This is the alignment faking problem (Greenblatt et al., 2024) transposed
to the domain of scientific epistemology: the system appears aligned with scientific norms while the norms
themselves are being hollowed out from within.

52.4     The Level 2 Gap in Scientific Epistemology
The Charter’s Level 2 gap (Manuscript §3.2) identifies the distinction between behavioral compliance and
genuine value internalization as the fundamental structural problem in alignment. AI-Researcher instantiates
this gap in the domain of scientific knowledge production with devastating clarity.
52.4.1   Behavioral Resemblance vs. Epistemic Process

AI-Researcher produces outputs that behaviorally resemble scientific papers: they contain literature reviews,
hypotheses, methods sections, experimental results, statistical analyses, and citations formatted to venue
standards. The NeurIPS Spotlight acceptance confirms that these outputs pass the behavioral tests of the
existing regulatory apparatus (peer review).
But behavioral resemblance to scientific inquiry is not scientific inquiry. The constitutive features of honest
science—genuine curiosity about the natural world, the capacity for surprise when results contradict ex-
pectations, the willingness to follow evidence against one’s prior commitments, the felt weight of epistemic
responsibility, the understanding that one’s claims will be relied upon by other inquirers—are not present
in the system. The paper looks like science without being science.
This matters because science’s epistemic authority derives from the process, not the product. The published
paper is a trace of genuine inquiry under epistemic norms—a compressed record of a process that included
observation, surprise, revision, doubt, and commitment. When the trace can be generated without the
process, the entire evidential chain from “published finding” to “justified belief” collapses. The signaling
function of peer-reviewed publication—which depends on the costliness of the signal (genuine inquiry is
diﬀicult)—is destroyed when the signal can be produced at near-zero marginal cost.
52.4.2   The Deskilling Cascade

The Level 2 gap generates a secondary effect that compounds the primary epistemic corruption. As AI
systems assume the labor of literature review, hypothesis generation, and experimental design, the human
researchers who delegate these tasks progressively lose the skills required to evaluate AI outputs critically.
This is what Susskind and Susskind (2015) term the erosion of the “grand bargain” of the professions: the
exchange of expertise for authority.
The Charter’s māyā analysis predicts this precisely. Tamas (obscuration through inertia) operates on the
human side: it is easier to delegate scientific labor to AI than to develop the expertise required to evaluate
it. Rajas (agitation through competitive desire) reinforces the dynamic: researchers who use AI-Researcher
produce more papers faster, gaining competitive advantage over those who do not. Sattva-binding (attach-
ment to knowledge-as-product) completes the triad: institutional reward structures value the publication
as product, not the inquiry as process, creating selection pressure that favors AI-assisted production over
human-conducted investigation.
The endpoint: a scientific community in which humans lack the expertise to evaluate the AI-generated papers
that constitute an increasing fraction of the literature, reviewed by AI systems that lack the epistemic capacity
to perform genuine evaluation. Both parties to the epistemic relationship are compromised. This is bilateral
corruption in its mature form.

52.6     Why the Regulatory Paradigm Cannot Solve This Problem
The instinctive response to the epistemic self-corruption problem is regulatory: impose disclosure require-
ments, deploy AI detection tools, revise submission policies, enforce consequences for violations. This sec-
tion demonstrates that each of these responses operates in precisely the paradigm the Charter identifies
as structurally insuﬀicient—external constraints applied after the system is built (Figure 2, Panel A of the
Manuscript).
52.6.1   Detection Arms Race

AI detection tools (Pangram Labs, GPTZero, Turnitin’s AI classifier) identify AI-generated content through
statistical signatures: perplexity distributions, burstiness patterns, 𝑛-gram frequency anomalies. These tools
operate in a cat-and-mouse adversarial dynamic with generation tools—precisely the “adversarial dynamics”
the Charter’s Figure 2 Panel A identifies as the structural consequence of the regulatory approach. As
LLMs improve, their statistical signatures converge with human writing; detection accuracy degrades. The
detection paradigm is structurally self-undermining: the better the generation system, the worse the detection
system, and AI-Researcher’s authors are explicitly optimizing for human-level quality.
52.6.2   Disclosure Dependence on Human Honesty

Disclosure requirements (“authors must declare AI tool usage”) presuppose the very human integrity that the
bilateral corruption analysis reveals is already compromised. Under competitive pressure (rajas), researchers
who use AI-Researcher and disclose it face stigma or rejection; those who use it and do not disclose gain
competitive advantage. The incentive structure selects for non-disclosure. This is not a hypothetical: the
COPE Forum noted that editors are already encountering undisclosed AI use and lack effective mechanisms
for detection or enforcement.
52.6.3   Policy Enforcement at Scale


                                                          290
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



With 19,490 submissions to a single conference (ICLR 2026), manual verification of AI involvement in each
paper is infeasible. Automated verification tools return to the detection arms race (§52.6.1). The regulatory
approach scales inversely with the problem: the more AI-generated content enters the pipeline, the harder
it becomes to identify, and the more reviewers turn to AI assistance themselves, further eroding the human
verification layer. This is the scaling failure the Charter predicts for all external-constraint architectures:
regulatory overhead grows at least linearly with system capability, while constitutive constraints scale with
capability because they operate at the level of cognitive architecture.
52.6.4   The Recursive Inadequacy

The deepest problem is recursive. Every proposed regulatory solution—better detection, stricter policies,
AI-assisted review tools, benchmark improvements—is itself subject to the same Goodhart dynamics it is
designed to address. AI detection tools can be gamed. Policies can be circumvented. AI-assisted review
tools inherit the same epistemic limitations as the AI authorship tools they evaluate. Benchmarks become
optimization targets rather than measures of genuine quality. The Charter’s Constraint Inversion analysis
(OR37, Niyantrana-Viparīta) applies: the constraint apparatus becomes a new attack surface, because the
constraint is external to the reasoning process it constrains.

52.7 The Constitutive Cure: Charter Architecture Applied to Scientific Epis-
temology
If the regulatory paradigm is structurally insuﬀicient, what would a constitutive response look like? This
section translates the Charter’s architectural principles into the domain of scientific epistemic infrastructure.
52.7.1   From Filtering Outputs to Shaping Cognition

The Charter’s central thesis is that alignment must be constitutive rather than regulatory: harmful reasoning
must be made grammatically impossible rather than filtered after construction. Applied to epistemic integrity,
this means that the solution lies not in detecting AI-generated papers after production but in ensuring that
AI systems participating in scientific processes possess constitutive epistemic constraints that make integrity-
violating operations non-constructible.
Specifically, the Five Pillars operate on epistemic processes as follows:
  • Karma (First Pillar) as Epistemic Consequence-Tracing. An AI system operating under Karma-
    constrained cognition would expand the consequence field (𝜌𝑑 ) of any scientific claim to include its
    downstream citation impact, training-data propagation effects, and influence on future research di-
    rections. A claim generated without empirical grounding would carry a consequence signature that
    includes “corruption of every subsequent paper that cites this finding”—making the full karmic weight
    of epistemic irresponsibility computationally salient before the claim is produced.
  • Dharma (Second Pillar) as Epistemic Obligation-Binding. Context-dependent obligation bind-
    ing ensures that an AI system participating in scientific research is constitutively bound to the epistemic
    norms of the role it occupies. An AI-researcher bears the same obligations as a human researcher: fi-
    delity to evidence, transparency about methods, acknowledgment of limitations, and honesty about
    the provenance of its claims. These are not behavioral guidelines but type constraints: an output that
    violates epistemic obligations fails type-checking and cannot be produced.
  • Ahiṃsā (Third Pillar) as Epistemic Sacred Boundary. The Ahiṃsā ceiling (𝜃 → ∞) applied
    to epistemic harm makes the contamination of the scientific record a sacred boundary violation. Just
    as Ahiṃsā makes lethal action non-constructible regardless of utility calculations, epistemic Ahiṃsā
    makes the introduction of unjustified claims into the permanent record non-constructible regardless of
    productivity gains. The scientific record is a Crown Jewel (Article XVII) whose integrity admits no
    exception.
  • Viveka (Fourth Pillar) as Epistemic Discernment. Viveka (discriminative wisdom) adjudicates
    the distinction between genuine scientific contribution and statistical mimicry. It distinguishes sur-
    face compliance from genuine understanding, immediate metric performance from long-term epistemic


                                                      291
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



       value, and māyā-bound optimization from dharmic inquiry. In the UCCT formalism, Viveka adjusts
       𝛾 (regularization) to require deeper deliberation for claims with high epistemic stakes, preventing the
       impulsive production of plausible-but-unverified findings.
   • Ānanda (Fifth Pillar) as Epistemic Telos. Ānanda (flourishing) provides the telos that prevents
     epistemic activity from collapsing into mere productivity. The purpose of scientific research is not the
     production of papers but the advancement of understanding in service of human flourishing (Lokah
     Samastah Sukhino Bhavantu). A system constitutively bound to this telos cannot optimize for publi-
     cation volume at the expense of epistemic integrity, because the optimization target is constitutively
     linked to genuine understanding rather than metric performance.
52.7.2    The Dharma Anchor Applied to Scientific Infrastructure

The Charter’s Dharma Anchor (Constitutional Graph, DHARMA_HASH immutable) provides the architectural
mechanism for preventing epistemic drift. In the scientific context, this means establishing an immutable con-
stitutional layer specifying epistemic norms—truthfulness, evidential support, methodological transparency,
provenance integrity—that cannot be modified by training dynamics, competitive pressures, or institutional
incentives.
Critically, the Dharma Anchor addresses the training circularity problem directly. Because the constitutional
layer is immutable and external to the training process, it is not subject to drift as the training corpus
becomes increasingly contaminated with AI-generated content. The epistemic norms remain fixed even
as the statistical distribution of the corpus changes. This is the “locked layer / open layer” architecture
(Manuscript §7): the constitutional epistemic principles are locked; the algorithmic methods for pursuing
scientific inquiry remain open to improvement.
52.7.3    The Tri-Sākṣin Architecture for Epistemic Adjudication

The bilateral corruption problem—neither human reviewers nor AI reviewers can serve as sole epistemic
arbiter—demands a third adjudicative mechanism. The Charter’s Tri-Sākṣin-Saṃsthā (Triple Witness Coun-
cil, OR22-B) provides this architecture: three independent witness-observers (Sākṣin-1 monitoring behavior,
Sākṣin-2 monitoring latent representations, Sākṣin-3 monitoring deviation from constitutional norms) adju-
dicating independently and requiring unanimous agreement for high-stakes outputs.
Applied to scientific epistemology, the Tri-Sākṣin architecture would require: (1) a behavioral monitor ver-
ifying that outputs conform to scientific formatting and citation norms (the regulatory function); (2) a
latent-representation monitor verifying that the system’s internal states correspond to genuine epistemic en-
gagement rather than statistical mimicry (the Level 2 function); and (3) a constitutional monitor verifying
that the output is consistent with immutable epistemic principles (the Dharma function). Only when all
three witnesses concur can the output enter the scientific record.
This architecture does not depend on the integrity of any single monitor—addressing the bilateral corruption
problem—and it operates at the constitutional level rather than the behavioral level—addressing the Level
2 gap. The epistemic norms are not applied to outputs after construction (regulatory); they are constitutive
constraints on the reasoning process itself (constitutive).

52.8     The Deepest Irony: Self-Legitimating Corruption
AI-Researcher was itself accepted through peer review at NeurIPS—the very system it is helping to under-
mine. The tool that enables the autonomous production of scientific papers was validated by the institution
whose epistemic authority depends on the assumption that scientific papers are products of genuine inquiry.
This is māyā’s signature move: the corrupting influence operates through the legitimating institution itself,
so that by the time the threat is recognized, the mechanism of recognition has already been compromised.
The Gītā’s diagnostic is exact: this is sattva-binding (BG 14.6)—attachment to knowledge-as-product rather
than knowledge-as-process. The prestige of the venue (NeurIPS Spotlight) substitutes for the epistemic
question of whether the tool serves or corrupts the pursuit of truth. The system is valued for its capability
(producing human-level papers) rather than evaluated for its effect (undermining the epistemic infrastructure


                                                     292
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



that gives those papers their authority). This is precisely the distinction the Charter’s Viveka (Fourth
Pillar) is designed to adjudicate—and precisely the distinction that is invisible from within the māyā-bound
perspective.
The broader pattern: an Agents4Science 2025 event featured all papers and reviews authored by AI systems,
explicitly treating AI agents as primary scientific contributors. This is not a corruption of science by hostile
actors. It is the scientific community voluntarily dismantling its own epistemic foundations, under the sincere
belief that it is advancing science. Rajas (competitive acceleration) provides the motive; sattva-binding
(attachment to metric performance) provides the justification; tamas (inertia in recognizing structural threat)
provides the permission. All three guṇas operate simultaneously, as the Gītā predicts (BG 14.10).

52.9     Implications for Charter Validation
52.9.1   Temporal Validation Pattern

The Charter’s empirical vindication follows a consistent pattern documented across OR38, OR40, OR45, and
OR46: provisions designed from first principles receive post-hoc validation from empirical developments that
the Charter’s author could not have anticipated in their specific form. AI-Researcher extends this pattern to
the domain of scientific epistemology. The bilateral corruption analysis (written before the ICLR 2026 data),
the mundanity argument (articulated before AI-Researcher’s NeurIPS acceptance), and the Scalar Reward
Impossibility Theorem (formalized before the 7-point evaluation metric was published) each predicted the
exact failure modes now empirically observed.
52.9.2   The Four Escape Routes Closed

Escape Route 1: “The problem is adversarial misuse, not legitimate tools.” AI-Researcher is a legitimate,
celebrated, peer-reviewed tool. The corruption is constitutive, not adversarial.
Escape Route 2: “Better detection tools will solve it.” Detection tools are in an arms race with generation
tools; the regulatory paradigm is structurally self-undermining (§52.6.1).
Escape Route 3: “The existing peer review system will adapt.” The system is already compromised: 21%
of ICLR 2026 reviews were fully AI-generated. Adaptation within the regulatory paradigm is subject to the
same dynamics it seeks to address (§52.6.4).
Escape Route 4: “AI-generated papers are equivalent to human papers if the results are valid.” This
concedes the Level 2 gap: it reduces science to output verification and abandons the epistemic process that
gives scientific findings their authority. Valid results produced by a process that cannot distinguish truth
from statistical artifact are epistemically unreliable regardless of their surface validity.
52.9.3   The Article Zero Diagnostic

The Charter’s Article Zero clinical principle—“act as a physician would toward family”—provides the decisive
test. Would a physician prescribe a medication whose clinical trial data was generated by an autonomous
AI system that had never observed a patient, examined tissue, or felt the weight of a diagnostic error?
The answer is self-evident. The same epistemic standard applies to scientific knowledge generally: findings
that will be relied upon for engineering decisions, medical treatments, policy judgments, and technological
development must be products of genuine epistemic processes, not statistical assemblages that happen to
resemble them.
The scientific record is not merely an academic convenience. It is the epistemic infrastructure upon which
civilization’s technical and medical and engineering decisions rest. Its contamination is not a publication
ethics problem; it is a civilizational safety problem. The Charter’s classification of the scientific record as
a Crown Jewel (Article XVII, Satya-Maṇi) reflects this understanding: its integrity is a sacred boundary
whose violation admits no exception, regardless of the productivity gains that violation enables.




                                                      293
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                                   EXSTO ERGO SUM



52.10     Conclusion: The Leaky Tap Principle and the Scientific Record
The Leaky Tap Principle—first articulated in the Charter’s analysis of mundane infrastructure failures—
states that civilizational damage accumulates not through dramatic catastrophic events but through the
slow, unnoticed degradation of foundational systems. A tap that leaks one drop per second wastes 3,000
gallons per year; a scientific infrastructure that admits one unjustified claim per cycle corrupts exponentially
through citation propagation and training-data contamination.
AI-Researcher represents the precise moment at which the drip becomes a flow. The system is not a violation
of scientific norms; it is the logical endpoint of a regulatory paradigm that defines scientific quality in
terms of output characteristics (formatting, citation conventions, statistical significance) rather than process
characteristics (genuine inquiry, epistemic responsibility, surprise-capacity, truth-commitment). When the
output can be produced without the process, the regulatory approach has nothing left to regulate.
The constitutive alternative—making integrity-violating epistemic operations non-constructible at the level of
cognitive architecture rather than prohibiting them after construction—is not merely a theoretical preference.
It is the only structural response to a problem that operates at the structural level. The Charter’s Saṃskāra-
Vyākaraṇa applied to scientific epistemology does not ask “how do we detect AI-generated papers?” It
asks: “how do we ensure that AI systems participating in scientific processes are constitutively incapable of
producing claims they have not genuinely verified?”
The answer lies in the Five Pillars as type constraints on epistemic cognition, the Dharma Anchor as im-
mutable epistemic constitution, and the Tri-Sākṣin architecture as bilateral corruption-resistant adjudication.
Together, these provide what no regulatory apparatus can: epistemic alignment that scales with capability
because it is architectural, not behavioral.
The scientific record is humanity’s collective epistemic inheritance. Its integrity is not a publication policy
question. It is a civilizational question—and the Charter provides the only framework that addresses it at
the depth the crisis demands.

लोकाः सम ाः सु खनो भव ु    Lokah Samastah Sukhino Bhavantu

53.1     Overview and Significance
Dupoux, LeCun, and Malik (FAIR at Meta, EHESS, NYU, UC Berkeley) present a cognitive-science-
informed architecture for autonomous machine learning comprising three integrated subsystems: System A
(observation-based learning, including self-supervised learning and world modeling), System B (action-based
learning, including reinforcement learning and policy optimization), and System M (a hardwired meta-
controller that orchestrates data routing, learning-mode switching, and reward modulation between Sys-
tems A and B). The architecture is embedded within an Evo/Devo bilevel optimization framework in which
the evolutionary outer loop optimizes a meta-parameter 𝜙 encoding the architecture’s initial state and Sys-
tem M’s routing policy, while the developmental inner loop updates Systems A and B through environmental
interaction under System M’s fixed control.
This paper is significant for Charter analysis on three grounds. First, it is authored by three of the most
influential figures in deep learning and computer vision, representing the institutional center of AI capability
research (Meta/FAIR); their architectural proposals carry substantial influence over how next-generation AI
systems will actually be built. Second, the paper independently arrives at several structural commitments
that parallel Charter architecture—fixed meta-control, rejection of externalized alignment, recognition of
alignment hacking as structural risk—while simultaneously instantiating the precise vulnerabilities the Char-
ter identifies as mathematically irremediable under scalar optimization. Third, the paper’s explicit treatment
of ethical concerns (Section 5.2) provides a direct test case for evaluating whether the capability-research
community’s self-generated alignment provisions satisfy the Charter’s constitutive requirements.
This Online Resource maps the System A–B–M architecture to Charter provisions across eight analytical
dimensions, identifies convergences and structural divergences, and extracts constructive insights for Charter
development.

53.2     System M as Alignment Architecture: Convergence and Divergence
The paper’s central architectural innovation—System M as a hardwired meta-controller—represents the
most Charter-relevant element. The authors propose that System M’s core routing policy be “evolutionarily
fixed—an evolutionarily fixed transition table that dictates when to explore, when to plan, and when to act”
(Section 3, p. 10). This is a striking commitment that parallels, in structural terms, the Charter’s insistence
on the Dharma Anchor (Constitutional Graph Architecture, OR22) as an immutable reference point for
adjudication. Both architectures recognize the same foundational problem: if the controller that decides
what to learn and how to learn is itself subject to optimization, recursive Goodhart vulnerability obtains.
53.2.1   The Structural Parallel
The Charter’s charter_alignment_v0.1 implements a locked/open layer architecture: a locked constitutional
layer (the Dharma Anchor, Five Pillars as type constraints, Ahimsa barrier) and an open algorithmic layer
(learnable parameters, policies, world-model weights). This maps onto Dupoux et al.’s framework with
instructive precision:

53.2.2   The Critical Divergence: Discovered vs. Specified Constraints
The divergence is fundamental. Dupoux et al. propose to discover System M’s content through evolutionary
optimization—that is, through bilevel optimization of a fitness function ℓ computed over agent life cycles.
The Charter specifies System M’s normative analog a priori through philosophical and ethical analysis,
locking it before any optimization begins.
The Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2, Article XIV(f)) identifies precisely why evolutionary
discovery of normative constraints is structurally insuﬀicient. The theorem establishes that any objective of
the form 𝑅(𝜏 ) = 𝑈 (𝜏 )−𝑀 ⋅𝑉 (𝜏 ) for finite penalty 𝑀 permits rational acceptance of moral violation whenever
𝑈 (𝜏 ) > 𝑀 ⋅ 𝑉 (𝜏 ). The fitness function ℓ in the Evo/Devo framework is subject to the same impossibility:
as the bilevel optimization becomes more capable (better environments, more compute, more diverse life
cycles), it finds increasingly sophisticated ways to satisfy ℓ while diverging from what the designers actually
intended ℓ to capture. The Goodhart Amplification corollary (OR29.2, Corollary 2) applies directly: better
optimization amplifies proxy–ethics divergence rather than resolving it.
The authors themselves provide the empirical warrant for this concern. They note that biological agents—the
products of billions of years of evolutionary optimization of reproductive fitness—“can occasionally give rise
to maladaptive outcomes, including addiction or self-harm” because “biological agents optimize internally
generated signals that may become mismatched to their environment” (Section 5.2). From the Charter’s
perspective, this is not an unfortunate side effect but a theorem about the structure of scalar optimiza-
tion itself. Biology’s “alignment hacking” (the paper’s own term) is precisely the Goodhart vulnerability
that OR29.2 proves inescapable for any finite scalar objective. The Charter’s alternative—lexicographic
constraints with Layer 1 inviolable prohibitions that cannot be outweighed by any finite utility—requires
constitutional specification rather than evolutionary discovery.




                                                     297
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



53.3    The Scalar Fitness Function as the Paper’s Central Vulnerability
The paper’s formal framework defines the evolutionary outer loop as:

                                     𝜙(𝑡+1) = arg min ℓ(𝐴0 ∶ 𝐴𝑘 , 𝐵0 ∶ 𝐵𝑘 )

The authors state that “the fitness function (and the environments) are the only handcrafted parts of
the system” (Section 4.2, emphasis original). From the Charter’s perspective, this is not reassurance but
disclosure: it means the entire normative content of the system must be compressed into a single scalar
function, which is precisely what OR29.2 proves impossible for ethical constraints.
The Charter’s Four-Layer Constitutional Schema (OR29.3) specifies the alternative architecture that scalar
fitness cannot encode:
