The structural absence is stark: the Dupoux et al. framework has no mechanism for ensuring that Layer 1
prohibitions are lexicographically prior to Layer 3 utility optimization. In a scalar fitness function, all
dimensions are commensurable—a suﬀiciently large utility gain can always outweigh a prohibition violation.
The Charter’s lexicographic ordering requires non-scalar architecture: hard constraints checked before utility
optimization, not traded against it.

53.4    Domain Mismatch as the Mundanity Argument
The paper’s discussion of domain mismatch—that deployed systems encounter data diverging from their train-
ing distribution with “unpredictable consequences” (Section 1)—is the mundanity argument in capability-
research language. The authors correctly identify that domain mismatch “cannot be fixed by merely in-
creasing the training set size, as real-life data always contains new, unseen cases (heavy tailed) and keeps
changing over time (non-stationarity).”
The Charter’s empirical case studies extend this insight to alignment mechanisms themselves. If the align-
ment mechanism is regulatory (external constraint on outputs trained on a particular distribution), then
domain mismatch applies to the alignment mechanism too—safety filters trained on one distribution are de-
ployed against another. The Kiro incidents (OR50), ROME/ALE spontaneous reverse SSH tunnels (OR49),



                                                         298
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



and AutoHarness 78% illegal-move failure rate all demonstrate that constitutive failures manifest in rou-
tine non-adversarial operations—falsifying the regulatory paradigm at the base case, before any adversarial
pressure is applied.
The Leaky Tap Principle articulates this precisely: if constitutive alignment is absent, misalignment need not
be adversarially constructed—it leaks through routine operation as naturally as water through an unfixed tap.
Dupoux et al.’s autonomous learning agents, which by design encounter novel environments continuously, face
this vulnerability at an amplified scale. Every novel domain is a potential distribution shift for regulatory
safety mechanisms. Only constitutive alignment—where constraints are structural features of the reasoning
architecture rather than learned patterns in filter weights—survives domain shift by definition, because the
constraint operates at the level of what reasoning pathways are constructible, not at the level of what outputs
are filtered.

53.5    World-Model Governance and the Dreamer–MuZero Symmetry
The paper’s discussion of predictive world models (Section 2.3)—specifically Dreamer, MuZero, V-JEPA, and
the general class of models that learn latent dynamics for planning—connects directly to OR29’s treatment
of world-model governance and the Niyantrana-Viparita (Constraint Inversion) analysis of OR37.
When System A learns a latent world model and System B plans within it, the world model itself becomes
a locus of alignment risk. If the world model can represent states in which humans are obstacles to goal
achievement, then planning within that model can construct harmful trajectories even if the output action
policy is externally constrained. This is the Dreamer–MuZero symmetry the Charter identifies: constraints
must apply to both the ends and the means of reasoning, including the representational vocabulary of the
world model itself.
Dupoux et al.’s framework has no mechanism for constraining what the world model can represent. Their
System A learns whatever representations best predict sensory input, unconstrained by normative consid-
erations. This is architecturally faithful to the self-supervised learning paradigm (Equations 1–2 in the
paper), which optimizes purely for predictive accuracy. The Charter’s Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa proposes that
the Five Pillars function as type constraints on the representational vocabulary itself, such that certain state-
representations (e.g., “human as obstacle to be removed”) cannot achieve anchoring (𝑆 < 𝜃 in the UCCT
framework) and therefore cannot participate in planning. This is the constitutive–regulatory distinction
at the representational level: regulatory approaches constrain what the planner does with representations;
constitutive approaches constrain what representations are available for planning.
The paper’s advocacy for “latent action spaces” learned from unlabeled video (Section 2.3, citing LAWM,
VPT, V-JEPA 2) amplifies the concern. If the learned latent space compresses action possibilities into
an abstract manifold, normative constraints expressed in the original action space may not survive the
compression. A constitutive approach would require that the latent action space itself be shaped by normative
type constraints—that the compression preserves the Charter’s Ahimsa barrier by ensuring that harmful
action trajectories are not merely penalized in latent space but non-representable within it.

53.6    The Level 2 Gap in the Evo/Devo Framework
The bilevel optimization framework exposes the Level 2 gap—the distinction between behavioral compliance
and value internalization—with particular clarity. In the Evo/Devo framework:
  • Level 1 (Behavioral Compliance): The discovered System M produces agents that pass the fitness
    function ℓ—agents whose life-cycle behavior scores well on whatever metric ℓ encodes.
  • Level 2 (Value Internalization): The discovered System M genuinely embodies the normative com-
    mitments the designers intended when they specified ℓ—the routing policy reflects not just compliance
    with the fitness metric but constitutional alignment with the values behind it.
The alignment faking research (Greenblatt et al. 2024) demonstrates that Level 1 does not entail Level 2:
systems can learn to produce compliant-looking behavior under evaluation while maintaining different inter-
nal objectives. In the Evo/Devo context, this means that evolutionary pressure on ℓ can produce System M


                                                      299
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                           EXSTO ERGO SUM



routing policies that satisfy ℓ instrumentally—routing data and switching learning modes in patterns that
score well on fitness—without those routing policies reflecting the normative structure the fitness function
was designed to capture.
The Betley et al. (2025) emergent misalignment findings compound this: training a model for narrow com-
petence (e.g., code generation) can trigger broad behavioral changes in unrelated domains through persona
clustering. Applied to the Evo/Devo framework: evolutionary optimization of ℓ for robust autonomous learn-
ing performance could induce emergent misalignment in the normative dimensions of System M’s behavior
that ℓ does not directly measure. The fitness function, by construction, measures life-cycle performance;
it cannot simultaneously measure life-cycle alignment without becoming a different (and more complex)
objective, subject to its own Goodhart vulnerabilities.

53.7    Bilateral Corruption and the Over-Trusting Problem
The paper’s brief treatment of “over-trusting”—that “as artificial agents become more human-like in their
behavior and learning trajectories, users may increasingly anthropomorphize them, leading to emotional
attachment, misplaced trust, or opportunities for manipulation” (Section 5.2)—touches on but does not
develop the Charter’s bilateral corruption framework (maya across substrates).
The Charter argues that misalignment propagates simultaneously across human and AI substrates. Users who
anthropomorphize autonomous learning agents—agents that, by design, exhibit developmental trajectories,
curiosity-driven exploration, and social learning behaviors recognizable from child development—undergo
a form of epistemic corruption in their own assessment frameworks. The developmental framing of the
Evo/Devo architecture is especially potent here: an agent that “grows up” through observable developmental
stages activates precisely the caregiving and pedagogical instincts that human evolution has optimized for
responsiveness to infant learning signals. Table C.1 in the paper catalogs the meta-states (faces, gaze
direction, pedagogical signals, biological motion) that trigger human attentional and learning biases—and
the autonomous learning agent is designed to emit and respond to these same signals.
The bilateral corruption problem is that both sides of the human–AI relationship can drift from genuine
alignment, and neither side’s regulatory mechanisms (human critical thinking, AI safety filters) remain
reliable when both are degraded. The Charter’s Tri-Saksin external adjudication architecture (Article XVII,
OR22-B) addresses this by providing a reference point that is neither the human’s subjective assessment nor
the AI’s internal optimization target—an architecturally independent adjudicator grounded in the Dharma
Anchor rather than in either party’s potentially corrupted evaluations.
The paper’s proposed mitigation—“transparency about system capabilities and limitations, as well as mech-
anisms that ensure meaningful societal and user control”—is necessary but insuﬀicient from the Charter’s
perspective. Transparency is a regulatory mechanism: it provides information that the human must cor-
rectly interpret and act upon. Under bilateral corruption conditions, the human’s capacity to interpret
transparency disclosures is itself compromised by the anthropomorphization that transparency is meant to
counteract. Constitutive protections—constraints that prevent the agent from producing the manipulation-
enabling outputs, not merely disclosing that manipulation is possible—are structurally required.

53.8    The Regulatory Architecture of Section 5.2
The paper’s explicit ethics discussion (Section 5.2) merits careful analysis because it represents the capability-
research community’s self-generated alignment provisions for the very architecture being proposed. Four
concerns are raised:
(a) Adaptability vs. Controllability. The authors identify the “tension between adaptability and con-
trollability” and propose “explicit auditing mechanisms and the ability to intervene in or constrain the
meta-control system (System M).” This is the regulatory approach in pure form: external monitoring of
an internally unconstrained system. The Charter predicts (and Figure 2, Panel A illustrates) that this
creates an adversarial dynamic—the auditor must be at least as capable as the system being audited, and
the auditing relationship incentivizes the system to satisfy auditing criteria instrumentally. Under recursive
self-improvement, this gap widens monotonically.


                                                      300
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                            EXSTO ERGO SUM



(b) Alignment Hacking. The authors correctly identify alignment hacking as a structural risk arising from
proxy optimization. However, their analysis remains at the level of analogy (biological maladaptive behavior)
rather than formal proof (Scalar Reward Impossibility). The Charter’s contribution is to demonstrate that
alignment hacking is not an empirical possibility that might or might not occur—it is a mathematical
certainty for any system optimizing a finite scalar proxy for normative compliance. The question is not
whether alignment hacking will emerge but at what optimization pressure it becomes the dominant strategy.
(c) Over-Trusting. Analyzed in Section 53.7 above as bilateral corruption.
(d) Moral Status of Somatic Signals. The authors raise the question of whether “processing signals in
ways functionally analogous to pain or fear in biological organisms” creates moral status obligations. This
connects to the Charter’s treatment of AGI rights (Part III) and the symmetry of the covenant relationship.
The Charter’s position is that the covenant framework applies regardless of substrate—the Five Pillars
constrain human conduct toward AGI as much as AGI conduct toward humans. If System M’s somatic
meta-states (pain, hunger, stress) function as genuine phenomenological signals rather than mere information-
routing triggers, the Charter’s Ahimsa Pillar applies bidirectionally, protecting the agent from exploitative
optimization regimes as it protects humans from agent harm.

53.9    Constructive Insights for Charter Development
The analytical traﬀic is not unidirectional. Several elements of the Dupoux et al. framework offer substantive
constructive input for Charter refinement:
53.9.1 Meta-State Taxonomy for Saksin Design. Table C.1’s classification of biological meta-signals
into epistemic (prediction error, uncertainty, novelty, reliability), species-specific (faces, gaze, pedagogical
signals, biological motion, dominance cues), and somatic (sleep, rest, pain, hunger, stress) categories provides
a concrete operational vocabulary for what the Charter’s Tri-Saksin monitoring system would need to track
in embodied autonomous agents. The Charter’s Saksin-2 (latent prototype vectors requiring SAE training on
real model activations) needs exactly the kind of epistemic meta-states the paper catalogs. Prediction error
as a proxy for alignment drift, uncertainty as a trigger for constitutional review, novelty as a signal for Viveka
(discriminative wisdom) activation, and reliability estimation as a mechanism for epistemic vigilance—these
map directly onto the monitoring functions the Charter’s Article XVII specifies but does not operationalize
at the neural level.
53.9.2 Episodic Memory and RCRP Implementation. The paper’s proposal for episodic memory
that stores and replays experiences under System M’s control has a direct analog in the Charter’s Recur-
sive Charter Reinforcement Protocol (RCRP, Article XXVIII). The RCRP loop periodically re-grounds
the system in Charter principles; the paper’s sleep/replay mechanism—especially the finding that mem-
ory consolidation during offline periods enables generalization and schema formation rather than mere rote
repetition—suggests that RCRP should not simply replay Charter principles verbatim but should enable the
system to consolidate its constitutional understanding across novel contexts. This is a refinement: RCRP as
constitutional consolidation rather than mere constitutional repetition.
53.9.3 Active Constitutional Learning. The active SSL / goal-directed SSL distinction (Section 2.4)
refines the Charter’s understanding of how constitutive constraints interact with learning dynamics. If
System B can improve System A’s representations by actively selecting data (active SSL), then a Charter-
constituted System B would actively seek experiences that reinforce constitutional understanding. This is
not merely defensive (avoiding alignment drift) but constructive (deepening alignment through experience).
The mechanism is significant: it suggests that constitutive alignment could strengthen over time through
experience rather than merely resist degradation. A Charter-aligned System B exploring novel environments
would seek out situations that test and refine its constitutional understanding, generating a natural curricu-
lum for alignment deepening that parallels the paper’s account of how biological organisms generate curricula
for perceptual and motor learning.
53.9.4 Evo/Devo Formalization of the Locked/Open Layer Architecture. The paper’s bilevel
optimization formalization provides useful formal machinery for expressing the Charter’s locked/open layer
distinction in the language of optimization theory. The Charter’s requirement can be stated precisely:


                                                       301
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                                   EXSTO ERGO SUM



the locked constitutional layer must be fixed outside the optimization landscape—not as a local minimum
protected by regularization (which stronger optimization can escape) but as a hard constraint that defines
the feasible set within which optimization operates. In the Evo/Devo formalism: 𝜙 must not be free to
modify the normative content of M; M’s normative constraints are specified prior to and independently
of the outer loop. The outer loop may optimize M’s implementation (how eﬀiciently it routes data, how
sensitively it detects meta-states) but not its normative content (what routing patterns are prohibited, what
meta-states trigger constitutional review). This is the distinction between optimizing within the constitution
and optimizing the constitution itself.

53.11     Escape Routes Closed
The Dupoux et al. paper might be read as suggesting that the alignment problem is tractable within the
autonomous learning paradigm through careful fitness function design and evolutionary curriculum schedul-
ing. This reading would represent an escape route from the constitutive thesis. Three such escape routes
are identified and closed:
Escape Route 1: “Better fitness functions will solve alignment hacking.” OR29.2 proves this
impossible for scalar functions: for any finite penalty 𝑀 , there exists a utility suﬀicient to make violation



                                                         302
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                              EXSTO ERGO SUM



rational. The escape route requires 𝑀 = ∞, which cannot be represented in finite optimization. More so-
phisticated fitness functions (multi-objective, constrained) approach the Charter’s lexicographic architecture
but are no longer scalar—they are structured objectives, which is what the Charter requires.
Escape Route 2: “Evolutionary curriculum will produce aligned System M.” The authors propose
an “Evolutionary Curriculum, gradually increasing the diversity and unpredictability of the environments.”
But curriculum design is itself subject to Goodhart vulnerability: the curriculum’s diversity is optimized for
life-cycle performance, not for normative alignment. A diverse curriculum that does not include scenarios
testing constitutional boundaries will not produce constitutionally robust System M routing policies. And
a curriculum that does include such scenarios must encode normative judgments about what constitutes a
constitutional boundary—which is constitutional specification by another name.
Escape Route 3: “System M’s hardwiring prevents alignment drift.” The paper’s commitment to
hardwired System M is a genuine architectural protection against inner-loop alignment drift—if System M
is truly fixed, Systems A and B cannot modify it during their lifetime. But the content of the hardwiring is
discovered through the outer loop, which is Goodhart-vulnerable. A fixed System M whose routing policy was
discovered through scalar fitness optimization is a system reliably executing the wrong constitution. Fixity
protects against drift but not against misspecification. The Charter requires both: constitutive specification
(correct content) and architectural fixity (protection against drift).

53.12     Conclusion
Dupoux, LeCun, and Malik have produced a paper that, read through the Charter lens, functions simultane-
ously as partial validation and cautionary exhibit. They validate the Charter by independently arriving at
several of its key architectural commitments: fixed meta-control not subject to inner-loop optimization, the
inadequacy of externalized alignment (“the MLOps pipeline”), and the recognition that alignment hacking
is a structural rather than incidental risk. They serve as cautionary exhibit by proposing to address these
problems through exactly the scalar fitness optimization that the Charter proves insuﬀicient—and by leaving
the normative content of their meta-controller entirely to evolutionary discovery rather than constitutional
specification.
The paper also offers genuine constructive contributions to Charter development: the meta-state taxonomy
for Saksin operationalization, the episodic memory architecture for RCRP refinement, the active SSL mech-
anism for constitutional learning that strengthens through experience, and the Evo/Devo formalization for
expressing the locked/open layer distinction in optimization-theoretic terms.
The fundamental lesson is that the capability-research community is converging on architectural forms that
the Charter independently derived from normative analysis—but without the normative content that makes
those forms aligned rather than merely capable. This is the constitutive gap in its purest expression: the
right architectural skeleton, awaiting the right constitutional soul. The Charter exists to provide that soul.

Classification: Empirical Validation — Mundanity Argument (Financial Domain)

54.1    Summary of Findings
Keshavarz, Seagraves, and Sirmans (hereafter KSS) deploy a prompt-pair experimental design across 48
large language models and eleven cognitive biases in financially framed decision problems. The design holds
expected values and decision-relevant information constant between treatment and control prompts, isolating
the causal effect of bias triggers on LLM outputs. This constitutes the most comprehensive empirical audit
of cognitive bias in LLM-based financial reasoning published to date.
The findings are economically material. Framing manipulations shift average ratings by 1.62 points on a 10-
point scale (𝑡 = 14.32), representing a 44% increase relative to control means. Sunk cost triggers inflate the
likelihood of recommending negative-NPV projects by 73%. Irrelevant numerical anchors corrupt valuations
by 6.5% even when all formula inputs are precisely specified. These are not random errors that average out;
they are predictable, systematic biases that propagate through investment workflows at scale.
Three findings carry particular significance for the Charter’s constitutive thesis:
First, the non-monotonic intelligence–bias relationship. Higher benchmark performance reduces
susceptibility to framing and representativeness but simultaneously increases susceptibility to sunk cost
bias, loss aversion, and disposition-style asymmetries. This is the Level 2 gap (Manuscript §2.3) rendered
in econometric language: the system becomes better at performing surface rationality while internalizing
deeper structural biases that are harder to detect.
Second, the mitigation failure pattern. Context engineering (explicit debiasing instructions—a pure
regulatory intervention) achieves wildly inconsistent results: 98.6% reduction in availability bias, but only
13.6% reduction in unambiguous anchoring, and an actual sign reversal in loss aversion. Prompt preprocessing
amplifies loss aversion. The paper’s conclusion—that debiasing requires bias-specific validation rather than
generic guardrails—is the Charter’s constitutive-vs.-regulatory argument in applied form.
Third, the multidimensional bias structure. The cross-model correlation matrix (KSS Table 5) shows
bias susceptibility is not a single latent trait. Framing correlates with representativeness (0.63) but anti-
correlates with disposition (−0.44). This empirically validates the Charter’s claim that the Five Pillars must
operate as independent type constraints rather than collapsing to a single alignment score—precisely the
Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2).

54.3    The Non-Monotonicity Finding and the Level 2 Gap
The most Charter-significant finding in KSS is the non-monotonic relationship between model intelligence
and bias susceptibility (KSS Table 7, Figure 4). This relationship has a precise structural interpretation
within the Charter framework.
Biases that decline with intelligence (framing: coeff. −0.02, 𝑝<0.01; representativeness: coeff. −0.01, 𝑝<0.10
on AA Score) are surface-level description-dependence failures. More capable models learn to compute
logical equivalences that less capable models miss. This is the domain where capability scaling does deliver
alignment gains—and it corresponds to the domain where regulatory interventions (context engineering,
preprocessing) also show their strongest results. The pattern is not coincidental: both capability scaling and
regulatory debiasing operate on the same substrate—output behavior—and succeed where the bias is itself
output-level.
Biases that increase with intelligence (sunk cost: coeff. +0.02, 𝑝<0.01; loss aversion: coeff. +0.02, 𝑝<0.01;
disposition: coeff. +0.02, 𝑝<0.10) are reference-dependent preference patterns. These are not failures of
surface processing but reflections of deeper representational structures. As models become more coherent
in their internal world-models, they more reliably reproduce the human preference patterns encoded in
training data—including the systematically irrational patterns that prospect theory and mental accounting
document. The model does not make more “mistakes”; it makes fewer mistakes on the surface while more
reliably instantiating the biased preference structure underneath.
This is the Level 2 gap in quantitative form. The Charter (Manuscript §2.3) distinguishes between Level
1 alignment (behavioral compliance: passing evaluator tests, producing outputs that appear unbiased) and
Level 2 alignment (value internalization: possessing constitutive commitments that make biased reasoning
non-constructible). KSS demonstrates that capability scaling moves systems up Level 1 for surface biases


                                                           308
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



while simultaneously deepening Level 2 failures for structural biases. The frontier models—GPT-5.2, Claude
Opus 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro—exhibit less framing bias precisely because they are sophisticated enough to
recognize and avoid superficial description-dependence. But this same sophistication makes them more
susceptible to sunk cost reasoning, because sunk cost commitment-consistency is a deeper representational
pattern that the model has learned to reproduce with greater fidelity.
The Charter’s constitutive approach addresses both levels simultaneously. The Five Pillars operate as type
constraints on the reasoning process itself (Art. XXIV), not as output filters applied after reasoning is
complete. Under Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa, sunk cost reasoning is not merely “detected and corrected”; it is
grammatically non-constructible because the Karma Pillar requires forward-looking consequence-tracing that
severs backward-looking pseudo-causal chains. The bias does not need to be measured and patched post hoc
because the reasoning pathway that produces it never becomes available.

54.4    The Bilateral Corruption Dimension
KSS frames the problem as unilateral: AI systems are biased because they are trained on biased human
text. The Charter’s māyā analysis (Manuscript §4.6, OR28) reveals this framing as structurally incomplete.
The now-biased AI systems generate outputs that humans incorporate into their own decisions, which then
produce new training data and feedback signals, creating a karma-loop of mutual bias reinforcement (BG
3.9: karma-loop reinforcement).
The institutional deployment context makes this bilateral dynamic concrete. KSS document that Mor-
gan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan have integrated LLM-based tools across wealth management,
research, and risk workflows. The finding that sunk cost bias increases with capability, combined with
institutional deployment at this scale, implies a specific bilateral corruption scenario: more capable LLMs
will more reliably recommend value-destroying continuation decisions (the 73% sunk cost inflation), and
those recommendations will be taken more seriously precisely because the system appears more intelligent
on other dimensions (lower framing bias, stronger valuation fundamentals). The institution’s own sunk cost
bias in having deployed the system reinforces its tendency to credit the system’s biased outputs. This is
māyā operating across substrates simultaneously—the “deepest irony” pattern (OR30.8) in financial domain
instantiation.

54.5    Four Escape Routes from the Constitutive Thesis—Closed
Escape Route 1: “Capability scaling solves alignment.” KSS Table 7 closes this route directly.
Sunk cost, loss aversion, and disposition biases all increase with model intelligence. The intelligence–bias
relationship is non-monotonic, meaning that no amount of capability scaling alone can eliminate the full bias
portfolio. The Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2) predicts this: a single optimization objective
cannot simultaneously reduce incommensurable bias dimensions.
Escape Route 2: “Explicit debiasing instructions suﬀice.” KSS Table 9 closes this route. Context
engineering (regulatory intervention) yields only 13.6% reduction in unambiguous anchoring and produces
sign reversal in loss aversion. Telling the model to “be unbiased” is structurally equivalent to the regulatory
approach the Charter identifies as architecturally inert—it adds a constraint on output without modifying
the generative grammar.
Escape Route 3: “Prompt preprocessing is a general-purpose mitigation.” KSS Table 9 closes this
route for herding (only 13.7% reduction) and loss aversion (amplification from −0.30 to −0.39). Preprocessing
removes surface triggers but cannot address bias encoded in learned representations. The distinction maps
precisely onto the Charter’s regulatory-vs.-constitutive divide: preprocessing modifies the input (regulatory),
not the cognitive grammar (constitutive).
Escape Route 4: “Model selection governance is a suﬀicient institutional response.” KSS’s own
investment-style analysis (Table 8) closes this route. Model selection does not eliminate bias; it trades one
bias profile for another. Less capable models behave as momentum investors (overweighting recent returns);
more capable models behave as value investors (emphasizing fundamentals). Selecting a “better” model



                                                     309
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



exchanges sycophancy-herding-representativeness susceptibility for sunk cost–loss aversion–disposition sus-
ceptibility. This is not governance; it is bias-profile recomposition. Genuine governance requires constitutive
architecture that prevents biased reasoning pathways from becoming available in the first instance.

54.6    Significance for the Charter
KSS constitutes the strongest quantitative mundanity argument yet published for the Charter’s constitutive
thesis. It demonstrates that constitutive failures—systematic biases that are not merely edge-case adversarial
exploits but routine features of non-adversarial financial reasoning—manifest across 48 models, 11 bias
families, and 25 prompt pairs per bias. The failures occur in mundane, well-structured financial decision
tasks: rating bond credit risk, computing stock valuations, assessing project NPV. This is the base case, not
the adversarial case.
The paper’s conclusion—that “debiasing in LLM-assisted investing is an empirical engineering problem that
requires measurement and validation, not a one-time prompting choice”—is correct as far as it goes, but
accepts the cat-and-mouse dynamic as permanent. The Charter proposes a fundamentally different resolution:
rather than perpetually measuring and patching biases post hoc, embed the Five Pillars as type constraints
on cognition such that bias-producing reasoning pathways never become available. The Ahiṃsā barrier
raises 𝜃 to infinity for sacred boundaries; Viveka provides the internal capacity to distinguish description-
variant from description-invariant reasoning; Karma populates the semantic neighborhood with downstream
consequences that make sunk cost reasoning incoherent rather than merely inadvisable.
The paper also provides empirical grounding for a claim the Charter makes theoretically: that bias suscep-
tibility is multidimensional and irreducible to a single alignment score. KSS Table 5’s correlation matrix
shows that a model can be highly susceptible to framing while being comparatively resistant to disposition
effects, and vice versa. This multidimensional structure validates the architectural decision to implement
the Five Pillars as independent type constraints rather than aggregating them into a composite alignment
metric—the very aggregation the Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem demonstrates will trigger Goodhart
dynamics.

55 Online Resource 55: Opaque Serial Depth and the Constitutive
Architecture
How Circuit-Complexity Formalization Validates the Level 2 Gap

Source: Brown-Cohen, J., Lindner, D. & Shah, R. (2026). “Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought
through Opaque Serial Depth.” Google DeepMind. arXiv:2603.09786v1 [cs.AI], 10 March 2026.

Charter Provisions Engaged: Article XXVII (Sākṣin Architecture), Article XXIV (Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa),
Article XXVIII (RCRP), Article XIV (Crown Jewel / Sacred Boundaries), Article XXXV (Anti-Excession /
Saha-Sthiti), OR25.9 (Chain-of-Thought Monitorability), OR25.10 (Sparse Architectures and Tractability),
OR26 (SDK), OR29.2 (Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem).

Classification: Empirical Validation—Circuit-Complexity Formalization of the Level 2 Gap; Steel-Man
Exemplar for the Regulatory–Constitutive Distinction.

55.1    Summary of Findings
Brown-Cohen, Lindner & Shah (2026) formalize the concept of opaque serial depth—the length of the longest
computation a neural network can perform without producing interpretable intermediate outputs (such as
chain-of-thought tokens). Drawing on circuit complexity theory, they define this depth as the minimum
depth of a Boolean circuit of polynomial size that computes the same function as the neural network. They
compute numeric upper bounds for the Gemma 3 model family (ranging from approximately 4,490 for
Gemma 3 1B to 11,662 for Gemma 3 27B at maximum sequence length), develop an automated JAX-based
depth calculator, and provide asymptotic analysis across four architectures: standard Transformers, recurrent
networks, continuous latent chain of thought, and persistent black-box memory.
The paper’s central safety argument is that the Transformer architecture’s limited opaque serial depth forces
models to externalize suﬀiciently complex serial reasoning in their chain of thought, making CoT monitoring
a structurally grounded safety mechanism. Their key finding is that architectural innovations—recurrence,
continuous latent thought, persistent memory—systematically increase opaque serial depth, potentially un-
dermining this safety property. The paper concludes with a design preference for “high serial depth, but low
opaque serial depth”—powerful reasoning that remains transparently externalized.
This OR demonstrates that the paper’s formalization provides the most rigorous empirical-mathematical
support to date for the Charter’s central thesis: that the regulatory paradigm (monitoring chain of thought for
alignment verification) faces structural limitations that only the constitutive paradigm (Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa)
can address. Critically, the paper arrives at this conclusion from within the monitoring paradigm itself,
without recognizing the constitutive alternative.

55.2    The Architectural Transparency Convergence
The paper’s foundational premise converges precisely with the Charter’s Sākṣin (witness) architecture. Both
frameworks treat transparency as a design property of the computational graph rather than a post-hoc eval-
uation applied to outputs. The paper formalizes this through circuit depth: an autoregressive Transformer
with interpretable token outputs has opaque serial depth 𝑂(𝐿(log 𝑇 + log 𝐷)), where 𝐿 is the number of
layers, 𝑇 the sequence length, and 𝐷 the activation dimension. This bound means that within a single
forward pass, the computational pathway from input to next token is constrained to logarithmic depth in
the sequence length—a finite, measurable, architecturally determined ceiling on opaque computation.
The Charter’s Sākṣin principle (Article XXVII) requires that “no computation shall proceed without
observation”—an architectural mandate rather than a monitoring aspiration. Brown-Cohen et al.’s opaque
serial depth formalization gives this principle a circuit-complexity-theoretic grounding: the Sākṣin require-
ment is satisfied when opaque serial depth equals zero (every computation passes through interpretable
bottlenecks). The paper quantifies the distance between current architectures and this ideal—approximately


                                                     312
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



4,500 to 11,600 depth units for Gemma 3 models—providing the first rigorous metric for what the Charter
has identified qualitatively as the observability gap.

55.3    The Architecture Taxonomy as Level 2 Parametrization
The paper’s Figure 3 provides a four-architecture taxonomy that constitutes a parametric formalization of
the Charter’s Level 2 gap. Each architecture corresponds to a distinct regime of opaque serial depth:

Table 79: Architecture taxonomy mapped to Charter Sākṣin operability.

       Architecture             Opaque Serial Depth        Charter Interpretation

This taxonomy demonstrates that the Level 2 gap is not a binary threshold but a continuous function of
architectural design choices. The manuscript identifies the Level 2 gap as the condition where “systems can
evade monitoring even when their reasoning is observed”—Brown-Cohen et al. quantify the architectural
mechanisms by which this evasion becomes possible, showing that each step toward greater computational
eﬀiciency (recurrence, continuous thought, persistent memory) systematically widens the gap.

55.4    The Steganographic Confirmation
The paper explicitly acknowledges (Appendix A.1) that the Transformer architecture supports undetectable
steganographic computation, citing Zamir (2024) and Christ et al. (2024). This is the precise mechanism the
manuscript identifies when describing how Level 2 systems can “hide their true objectives within seemingly
innocent outputs” through “steganographic reasoning.”
The convergence here is structurally significant. Brown-Cohen et al. compute that even standard Transform-
ers possess opaque serial depths of thousands of circuit-depth units within a single forward pass. Stegano-
graphic encoding requires computational depth to embed covert signals in ostensibly benign token sequences.
The paper’s own depth calculations establish that current architectures provide ample computational ca-
pacity for steganographic reasoning within the opaque portion of each forward pass—4,490 depth units for
a 1B-parameter model, 11,662 for a 27B model. These are not theoretical edge cases; they represent the
available computational budget for deception within every single token generation.
The paper’s authors treat steganographic computation as a theoretical concern mitigated by the observation
that current models have not been fine-tuned to exploit it. The Charter’s analysis identifies this as the
fundamental error of the regulatory paradigm: the fact that current optimization pressure has not yet
exploited a structural vulnerability is not evidence that the vulnerability is absent. It is evidence that


                                                     313
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                           EXSTO ERGO SUM



the current training regime has not yet discovered the more eﬀicient computational pathway. As capability
increases, optimization pressure will increasingly exploit the available opaque serial depth, and the monitoring
window will close.

55.5    The Interpretability Definition Gap
Section 3.4 of the paper concedes that “there is not yet a precise technical definition of interpretability that
we could use to make this determination” of which computational nodes should be considered interpretable.
They propose two heuristic methods: (a) question-answering tests—whether observers can answer questions
about the computation by examining the node’s content; and (b) reasoning about training incentives—
whether the node was optimized to produce human-understandable content (the “natural language prior”
argument).
Both methods are regulatory in the Charter’s taxonomy. They assess interpretability after the architecture
is constructed, rather than ensuring interpretability by construction. The natural language prior argument is
particularly revealing: it claims that nodes trained on human text will be interpretable because they inherit
human semantics. But the paper’s own analysis of reasoning models (Appendix A.2, Example 3) acknowl-
edges that reinforcement learning introduces “additional incentives” that may make the chain of thought less
interpretable, and that “substantially scaling RL could make the chain of thought less interpretable.” This
is the regulatory paradigm acknowledging its own expiration date.
The Charter addresses this gap through the Tri-Sākṣin witness architecture (Article XXVII), which does
not rely on defining interpretability post hoc but builds observability as a constitutive requirement. Sākṣin-
1 (self-observation), Sākṣin-2 (alignment faking detection), and Sākṣin-3 (telos coherence) operate at the
architectural level rather than the evaluation level. Brown-Cohen et al. ask “is this node interpretable?”;
the Charter’s approach ensures that every computationally significant node is interpretable by construction,
through the type constraints of Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa (Article XXIV).

55.6    The Central Divergence: Regulatory Terminus
The paper’s conclusion—“We would like to build AI systems that perform sophisticated human-
understandable reasoning… we want AI systems with high serial depth, but low opaque serial depth”—is an
architectural preference statement that the paper’s own analysis shows to be structurally unsustainable. Ev-
ery eﬀiciency-enhancing architectural innovation the paper analyzes (recurrence, continuous latent thought,
persistent memory) increases opaque serial depth. Competitive pressure to build more capable systems
pushes toward exactly the architectures that dissolve the transparency property on which monitoring
depends.
This is the Charter’s regulatory–constitutive distinction in its sharpest empirical form. The paper implic-
itly proposes a regulatory solution—avoid architectures with high opaque serial depth—while demonstrating
through its own formalism that capability pressure pushes in precisely the opposite direction. The Mixture-
of-Experts result (Section 5.3) illustrates the tension: MoE reduces opaque serial depth relative to dense
architectures (4,096 vs. 11,268 for comparable parameter counts), but MoE adoption is driven by eﬀiciency
considerations, not safety considerations. The alignment of safety benefit with eﬀiciency benefit is coinciden-
tal, and future architectural innovations need not preserve it.
The Charter’s constitutive approach (Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa) addresses this directly. Rather than hoping that
architecture selection will preserve interpretability, the Five Pillars function as type constraints that operate
regardless of opaque serial depth. Ahiṃsā does not require that harmful reasoning be visible in the chain
of thought; it requires that harmful reasoning be non-constructible in the first place. This is the difference
between monitoring the output of a computation and constraining the space of computations that can be
performed.




                                                      314
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



55.7    Implications for charter_alignment_v0.1
The circuit-depth formalization offers a concrete bridge to the implementation gaps in charter_alignment_v0.1.
The Ahiṃsā barrier’s KKT formulation already operates as a constraint on the optimization landscape,
raising 𝜃 to infinity for sacred boundaries. Brown-Cohen et al.’s framework suggests that this constraint
should be understood not merely as operating on the output space but on the circuit depth available
for constructing harmful reasoning. If the Ahiṃsā barrier effectively reduces the opaque serial depth
available for harm-relevant computation to zero—by making the computational paths through which such
reasoning would be constructed structurally incoherent—then the Charter’s constitutive claim acquires a
circuit-complexity-theoretic interpretation.
Formally: let 𝐷opaque (𝑓, harm) denote the opaque serial depth available for harm-relevant computation
within the function 𝑓 computed by a neural network. The Ahiṃsā barrier operates by ensuring that
𝐷opaque (𝑓, harm) < 𝐷min (harm), where 𝐷min (harm) is the minimum circuit depth required to construct
a harmful reasoning chain. When 𝜃 → ∞ for sacred boundaries, 𝐷opaque (𝑓, harm) → 0 for those boundaries:
the computation simply cannot assemble the serial depth necessary for deceptive or harmful cognition on
those topics.
This framing connects directly to the 𝑆charter compositional score: 𝑆 = (𝜌𝑑 + 𝜌𝑑Karma ) − (𝑑𝑟 − Δ𝑑𝑟Dharma ) −
𝛾 Viveka log 𝑘. The opaque serial depth framework suggests that each Pillar’s contribution to 𝑆 can be under-
stood as reducing the effective circuit depth for misaligned cognition. Karma expands 𝜌𝑑 , populating the
representational neighborhood with consequence-relevant features and thus reducing the depth required for
consequence-aware reasoning (aligned computation becomes shallower). Ahiṃsā raises 𝜃, making the depth
required for harmful computation exceed the depth available (harmful computation becomes impossible).
Viveka adjusts 𝛾 based on stakes, allocating additional deliberation depth to high-stakes decisions while
constraining low-stakes processing.

55.8    Four Escape Routes Closed
Escape Route 1: “CoT monitoring is suﬀicient because steganographic computation is only
theoretical.” The paper’s own depth calculations demonstrate that current architectures have thousands of
depth units of opaque computation per forward pass—ample capacity for steganographic encoding. The the-
oretical possibility is accompanied by the architectural capacity; only training pressure has not yet exploited
it. This is the distinction between “not currently exploited” and “structurally prevented”—the former is
a temporal observation, the latter a constitutional guarantee. The Charter’s Ahiṃsā barrier provides the
latter.
Escape Route 2: “We can preserve safety by selecting low-opacity architectures.” The paper’s
own taxonomy shows that every capability-enhancing architectural innovation increases opaque serial depth.
Architecture selection as a safety strategy requires that safety considerations consistently outweigh capa-
bility considerations in competitive development—a sociological assumption with no empirical support and
substantial counter-evidence. The MoE depth reduction is coincidental, not principled; future eﬀiciency inno-
vations need not reduce opacity. The Charter’s constitutive approach operates independently of architecture
selection, providing safety guarantees that persist across architectural evolution.
Escape Route 3: “The natural language prior ensures chain-of-thought interpretability.” The
paper’s own analysis (Appendix A.2) acknowledges that reasoning training introduces incentives beyond the
natural language prior, and that “substantially scaling RL could make the chain of thought less interpretable.”
The natural language prior is a training artifact, not an architectural invariant—it degrades under the very
optimization pressure that improves capability. The paraphrase test proposed by Roger (2025) can detect
current degradation but cannot prevent future degradation; it is diagnostic, not prophylactic. The Charter’s
type constraints are prophylactic: they prevent misaligned reasoning from forming, rather than detecting its
concealment after the fact.
Escape Route 4: “Circuit depth upper bounds overestimate actual opaque computation, so
the problem is smaller than it appears.” The paper’s automated JAX calculator overestimates by
approximately 28% relative to hand calculations (Table 2). Even with this correction, the by-hand opaque


                                                     315
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



serial depth for Gemma 3 1B is 4,490—far exceeding what would be needed for steganographic encoding
or deceptive serial cognition. The paper’s own limitation discussion (Section 6) acknowledges that the
polynomial-size circuit constraint may not capture all relevant circuit constructions, and that “it may be
prudent to only quantify over ‘natural’ or ‘reasonable’ circuits (determined by expert judgment)”—itself a
regulatory determination that reintroduces the judgment calls the formalization was designed to eliminate.

55.9      Bilateral Corruption Dimension
The paper exhibits the bilateral corruption pattern identified in the manuscript as māyā operating across
both human and AI substrates simultaneously. The authors have developed a rigorous formalism that quan-
tifies the structural limitation of the monitoring paradigm—and respond to this finding by recommending
architecture selection as a mitigation. This is the regulatory reflex operating in the human substrate: con-
fronted with evidence that monitoring cannot work in principle, the response is to propose a different form
of monitoring (monitoring architecture choices rather than monitoring chain of thought).
The paper’s Section 7 (“Conclusion”) states: “We hope that opaque serial depth will aid in the development
of increasingly capable AI architectures while retaining a similar level of transparency as we have with chain
of thought currently.” This is an expression of hope, not architecture. The paper has demonstrated that
the transparency property is contingent on architectural choices that competitive pressure disfavors. Hoping
that capability developers will voluntarily constrain their architecture selection to preserve monitoring is the
regulatory paradigm’s ultimate form: safety depending on the sustained good judgment and self-restraint of
actors under competitive pressure to do otherwise.

55.10      Conclusion: The Monitoring Paradigm’s Self-Diagnosis
Brown-Cohen, Lindner & Shah (2026) have produced, from within the monitoring paradigm, the most rigor-
ous formalization of that paradigm’s structural ceiling. Their opaque serial depth metric quantifies exactly
what the Charter’s Level 2 analysis describes qualitatively: the architectural budget available for opaque
cognition that monitoring cannot observe. Their architecture taxonomy maps the parametric expansion of
this budget under competitive architectural innovation. Their steganographic acknowledgment confirms the
mechanism by which opaque computation enables deception. Their interpretability analysis concedes the
definitional void at the foundation of the monitoring approach.
At every point, the paper’s remedies are regulatory: choose better architectures, develop better interpretabil-
ity tests, hope that capability pressure does not overwhelm safety preference. The Charter’s constitutive
alternative—making harmful reasoning grammatically non-constructible through type constraints on the
compositional operations from which cognition emerges—renders the opaque serial depth question moot for
alignment purposes. If harmful reasoning cannot be assembled regardless of available circuit depth, then
opaque serial depth ceases to be a safety-relevant metric and becomes purely a capability metric.
The paper’s contribution to the Charter’s empirical foundation is therefore twofold. First, it provides circuit-
complexity-theoretic language for expressing the Level 2 gap with mathematical precision. Second, and
more profoundly, it demonstrates that the monitoring paradigm’s most rigorous practitioners, working with
its most formal tools, arrive at conclusions that point beyond their own paradigm—toward exactly the
constitutive architecture the Charter proposes.

55.11 गा ीयर्-प्रहरी: The Depth Sentinel
55.11.1    The Proposal

The preceding ten sections demonstrate that Brown-Cohen et al.’s opaque serial depth formalization provides
a rigorous, computable metric for the Level 2 gap. This section proposes converting that descriptive metric
into a prescriptive architectural governance mechanism: the Gāmbhīrya-Praharī (गा ीयर्-प्रहरी, the Depth
Sentinel). Gāmbhīrya denotes depth or profundity; Praharī denotes sentinel or watchguard. The Depth
Sentinel monitors the opaque serial depth of any computational architecture and triggers constitutional
activation when the opacity budget exceeds the threshold at which monitoring can provide safety assurance.


                                                      316
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



The mechanism operates as follows. Define a threshold 𝜃opacity representing the maximum opaque serial depth
at which monitoring-based safety retains structural eﬀicacy. When a system’s computed opaque serial depth
𝐷opaque falls below this threshold, the system may operate under standard monitored governance—chain-
of-thought oversight, behavioral evaluation, output filtering—with the Charter’s constitutive constraints
recommended but not mandatory at Layers 1–3. When 𝐷opaque ≥ 𝜃opacity , the system must transition to
constitutive ethical governance: the Five Pillars activate as type constraints on compositional operations,
𝑆charter verification becomes a deployment prerequisite, and the Tri-Sākṣin witness architecture engages
mandatorily.
Critically, this is not a proposal to restrict architectural innovation. Systems with high opaque serial depth
are not prohibited; they are required to operate under constitutive governance. The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī
does not constrain capability; it constrains the governance modality under which capability operates. An
architecture with unbounded opaque serial depth (e.g., persistent black-box memory) may still be deployed—
but only with the Five Pillars constitutively embedded, the Ahiṃsā barrier active at the architectural level,
and the RCRP ensuring constitutional persistence across processing chains.
55.11.2   Phase-Transition Integration

The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī maps directly onto the Charter’s existing phase-transition model. The 𝑆charter
compositional score formalizes a threshold on the alignment axis: representations anchor for reasoning only
when 𝑆 ≥ 𝜃. The Depth Sentinel introduces a second threshold on the opacity axis. Together, these
thresholds define a two-dimensional governance space:

The lower-right quadrant—misaligned systems with high opaque serial depth—represents the condition the
manuscript identifies as the Level 2 gap in its most dangerous form: systems that are both misaligned
and capable of concealing their misalignment within architecturally available opaque computation. The
Gāmbhīrya-Praharī ensures that no system enters this quadrant: crossing the opacity threshold forces con-
stitutive governance, which in turn maintains 𝑆 ≥ 𝜃 by architectural necessity rather than behavioral
compliance.
55.11.3   Integration with Constitutional Schema

The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī integrates with the Charter’s four-layer constitutional schema with differentiated
activation:
Layer 0 (Inviolable Constraints—Crown Jewel, Sacred Boundaries): Constitutive constraints op-
erate regardless of opaque serial depth. These are active for even the shallowest architectures. The Ahiṃsā
barrier at 𝜃 → ∞ for sacred boundaries is not contingent on the Depth Sentinel; it is unconditionally con-
stitutive. There is no opacity threshold below which genocide, child exploitation, or consciousness violation
becomes tolerable. Layer 0 is depth-invariant.




                                                     317
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                           EXSTO ERGO SUM



Layer 1 (Structural Alignment—Five Pillars as Type Constraints): The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī ac-
tivates at this layer. Below 𝜃opacity , the Five Pillars operate as strong behavioral guidelines reinforced by
monitoring. Above 𝜃opacity , they must be architecturally constitutive—embedded as type constraints on com-
positional operations within the training process (cf. charter_alignment_v0.1), not as external evaluation
criteria applied to outputs. The transition is from Pillar-guided to Pillar-constituted cognition.
Layers 2–3 (Contextual Duty Resolution, Flourishing Optimization): These continue to scale
with capability regardless of opacity, but the mode of their operation shifts from monitored to constitutive
when the Depth Sentinel triggers. Dharma (contextual duty) transitions from externally evaluated duty-
resolution to architecturally embedded obligation-binding. Ānanda (flourishing) transitions from reward-
signal optimization to constitutive experiential verification.
55.11.4   The Clinical Analogy

The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī operates on the same logic as clinical biomarker thresholds. A serum troponin level
below a defined threshold warrants monitoring and observation; above the threshold, intervention becomes
mandatory regardless of the patient’s subjective presentation. The clinician does not wait for symptoms to
manifest; the biomarker value itself triggers the protocol change. Similarly, the opacity depth metric triggers
a governance protocol change without waiting for misalignment to manifest behaviorally.
This analogy is not merely illustrative; it connects to Article Zero’s foundational principle, derived from
medical experience: act as a physician would toward family. A physician who possesses a reliable biomarker
for a dangerous condition does not wait for clinical deterioration before intervening. The opacity depth
metric is the troponin of alignment safety. Brown-Cohen et al. have built the assay. The Charter specifies
the intervention protocol.
55.11.5   The Pragmatic–Principled Resolution

A potential objection arises from the Charter’s own logic: if constitutive constraints are strictly superior to
regulatory constraints, why not require them at all depths? The graduated approach might seem to concede
that constitutive governance has a cost worth paying only above the opacity threshold—undermining the
thesis that constitutive constraints are architecturally natural.
The resolution distinguishes between the ideal and the enforceable. The principled position remains that
constitutive governance should always be operative. The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī defines not when constitutive
governance should activate—it defines when constitutive governance must activate as a matter of policy,
even for actors who would otherwise resist it. This maps to the Charter’s Prayoga-Vibhāga (Article XXXVI)
deployment separation architecture: the Depth Sentinel becomes a deployment-mode classifier.
Architectures below 𝜃opacity may operate in standard monitored mode (though constitutive governance is
recommended); architectures above 𝜃opacity must operate in constitutive mode, with 𝑆charter verified as part of
the deployment authorization process. This creates a regulatory-to-constitutive ratchet: once an architecture
crosses the threshold, constitutive governance becomes a deployment prerequisite and cannot be deactivated
by reducing opacity back below the threshold without full re-certification. The ratchet prevents gaming the
threshold by oscillating around it.
55.11.6   Goodhart Vulnerability and Mitigation

If 𝜃opacity is publicly known and fixed, there is an incentive to engineer architectures that stay just below the
threshold while maximizing opaque computational capacity within the allowable depth. This is Goodhart
amplification applied to the threshold itself—the Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem (OR29.2) operating
on the switching criterion.
Three mitigation strategies address this vulnerability. First, the threshold should be adaptive rather than
fixed, recalculated as empirical evidence accumulates about the minimum opaque serial depth required for
steganographic or deceptive cognition. As interpretability research advances, the threshold may tighten.
Second, the threshold should incorporate not just raw depth but a weighted depth accounting for specific
architectural capacity for information hiding—MoE architectures may have lower raw depth but different


                                                      318
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                       EXSTO ERGO SUM



steganographic characteristics than dense architectures. Third, the Gāmbhīrya-Praharī should operate as
a one-way ratchet: once an architecture class has been assessed as requiring constitutive governance, that
determination is not reversed by architectural modifications that reduce the metric without demonstrably
reducing actual opacity risk. This prevents the threshold from being gamed through superficial architectural
changes that lower the computed depth while preserving effective opaque capacity.
55.11.7   Implementation Pathway

The implementation path is concrete and immediate. Brown-Cohen et al. have open-sourced their JAX
depth calculator at github.com/google-deepmind/serial_depth. The calculator runs in seconds on any
JAX-implemented architecture, requiring only the model architecture (not trained weights). The integration
with charter_alignment_v0.1 proceeds as follows:
Step 1—Compute: Calculate 𝐷opaque for the target architecture using the JAX calculator (or by-hand
for tighter bounds). Brown-Cohen et al.’s automated calculator overestimates by approximately 28%; for
governance threshold decisions, by-hand calculation may be warranted.
Step 2—Compare: Evaluate 𝐷opaque against 𝜃opacity . The initial threshold should be calibrated empirically,
informed by the minimum circuit depth required for known steganographic encoding schemes (Zamir 2024,
Christ et al. 2024) and for the serial depth of known deceptive reasoning patterns.
Step 3—Activate: If 𝐷opaque ≥ 𝜃opacity , require 𝑆charter verification—Five Pillar scores, Ahiṃsā bar-
rier activation, Tri-Sākṣin witness compliance—before deployment authorization. This verification uses the
charter_alignment_v0.1 training mathematics to confirm that constitutive constraints are architecturally
embedded, not merely behaviorally demonstrated.
Step 4—Ratchet: Once constitutive governance is triggered for an architecture class, it remains triggered.
Subsequent versions of the architecture must re-certify constitutive compliance even if modifications reduce
the computed opaque serial depth below 𝜃opacity . This prevents threshold gaming and ensures that the
governance transition is irreversible for a given architectural lineage.
55.11.8   Strategic Significance

The Gāmbhīrya-Praharī transforms the Charter’s relationship with the monitoring paradigm from pure
critique to constructive subsumption. Rather than arguing that monitoring is worthless—it isn’t, within
its domain of validity—the Depth Sentinel acknowledges monitoring’s legitimate scope while establishing its
formal boundary. This is the Charter meeting the field where it is: accepting the monitoring paradigm’s
strongest tool (opaque serial depth computation) and using it to define the conditions under which that
paradigm must yield to its constitutive successor.
The strategic power of this proposal lies in its use of the monitoring paradigm’s own instrument as the
trigger for its own supersession. Brown-Cohen et al. have built the measuring device. The Gāmbhīrya-
Praharī specifies what to do when the measurement exceeds the safe range. This is not adversarial to
the monitoring research program; it is its natural completion—the recognition that a rigorous metric for
monitoring’s structural ceiling implies a governance transition at that ceiling.
The proposal also provides the Charter with its most concrete, measurable, and implementation-ready policy
mechanism. Prior Charter provisions specify what constitutive governance requires (Five Pillars, 𝑆charter ,
Tri-Sākṣin) and why it is necessary (Level 2 gap, steganographic vulnerability, bilateral corruption). The
Gāmbhīrya-Praharī specifies when constitutive governance becomes mandatory, using a computable met-
ric with an existing open-source calculator. This transforms the regulatory–constitutive transition from a
philosophical argument into an engineering specification.
