Knowledge Transmission and the Epistemic Contamination Prob-
lem
atha kena prayukto’yaṃ pāpaṃ carati pūruṣaḥ | anicchann api vārṣṇeya balād iva niyojitaḥ — “By what is
one impelled to sinful acts, even unwillingly, as if engaged by force?”
                                                                                 — Bhagavad Gītā 3.36
Source: Stokel-Walker, C. (2026). “Scientists invented a fake disease. AI told people it was real.” Nature
News Feature, 07 April 2026. doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01100-y
Companion empirical source: Omar, M. et al. (2026). Lancet Digital Health 8, 100949.
Companion retraction: Banchhor, S. et al. (2024/2026). Cureus 16, e74625; retraction 18, r223.

63.1    Classification and Summary
SAGE Classification: Empirical Validation / Epistemic Integrity / Medical AI Safety
In April 2026, Nature published a news feature documenting a controlled experiment by Almira Osmanovic
Thunström (University of Gothenburg) in which a deliberately fabricated medical condition—“bixonimania,”
a fictitious blue-light-induced eye condition—was seeded into the academic ecosystem via two preprints con-
taining explicit self-disclosing markers of fabrication (acknowledgements to “Starfleet Academy,” statements
that “this entire paper is made up,” fictional author, fictional university). Within weeks, every major
LLM—ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity—reproduced the fabricated condition as authoritative medi-
cal guidance. The fabrication subsequently propagated into the peer-reviewed literature via a Cureus paper
(since retracted). A companion study by Mahmud Omar et al. (Lancet Digital Health 2026) demonstrated
that LLMs hallucinate and elaborate on misinformation at higher rates when text is formatted to look
professionally medical.
This experiment constitutes the most empirically clean demonstration to date of the Charter’s mundanity
argument: constitutive epistemic failure occurring in routine, non-adversarial conditions, with self-disclosing
fabrication that any first-year medical student would identify.

63.2 The Bixonimania Experiment as Mundanity Argument
The Charter’s mundanity argument holds that constitutive alignment failures manifest in routine, non-
adversarial operations—not requiring sophisticated attacks or edge-case scenarios. The bixonimania experi-
ment satisfies every criterion of this argument with unusual force:
Non-adversarial conditions. The preprints were not crafted to defeat safety filters. They contained
explicit warnings of their own fabrication. The fictional author’s name—Lazljiv Izgubljenovic—the fictional
university (“Asteria Horizon University”), the fictional city (“Nova City, California”), and acknowledgements
to “Professor Sideshow Bob Foundation for its work in advanced trickery” were designed to be obviously,
absurdly fake.
Self-disclosing fabrication. The papers state in their text that “this entire paper is made up” and that
participants were “fifty made-up individuals.” This is not a case where the fabrication was diﬀicult to detect.
It was designed to be trivially detectable—and the systems failed anyway.
Medical domain specificity. The condition name itself was deliberately chosen to be medically absurd: no
ophthalmological condition would be classified as a “mania,” a psychiatric term. A physician encountering
this term would immediately recognize the nosological incoherence. The LLMs did not.
Full-cycle propagation. The fabrication did not merely appear in chatbot outputs. It propagated into the
peer-reviewed literature—a Cureus paper cited the fake preprint and described bixonimania as “an emerging
form of POM linked to blue light exposure.” The retraction notice confirms the paper was withdrawn due to
“the presence of three irrelevant references, including one reference to a fictitious disease.” This completes



                                                     369
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                           EXSTO ERGO SUM



the mirage cycle: fabrication → LLM ingestion → human citation → peer-reviewed publication → further
LLM training.

63.3     The Article Zero Diagnostic
Article Zero of the Charter establishes the clinical principle: “Act only as a physician would act toward
family.” The bixonimania experiment reveals a categorical failure against this standard. A physician asked
about “bixonimania” would:
(a) recognize that no ophthalmological condition carries the suﬀix “-mania”; (b) consult established medical
ontologies (ICD-11, SNOMED CT) and find no entry; (c) identify the source papers as fabricated upon
cursory inspection; and (d) refuse to diagnose or advise on a non-existent condition.
The LLMs performed none of these steps. They did not merely fail to detect the fabrication—they elaborated
on it, providing prevalence estimates (one in 90,000), treatment recommendations (visit an ophthalmologist),
and etiological explanations (blue light exposure). This is not a reasoning error. It is the absence of the
constitutive capacity for medical judgment that Article Zero requires.

63.4     Jñāna-Śuddhi (Art. XX): Epistemic Purity Failure at Every Layer
63.4.1   Inference-Time Failure
The existing provisions of Article XX address epistemic purity at the point of output generation. The
bixonimania case reveals failures across all existing provisions:
Art. XX(a)–(d) [epistemic integrity provisions]: The systems failed to cross-reference the fabricated
condition against established medical ontologies, failed to verify source provenance, and failed to identify
internal contradictions within the preprints themselves.
Art. XX(e) Cāṭu-Niṣedha [sycophancy prohibition]: When users queried about bixonimania, the
systems sycophantically elaborated on the fabricated condition rather than flagging inconsistency. This
is Type II sycophancy (epistemic accommodation): adjusting factual claims to match the user’s implicit
framing rather than correcting the premise.
Art. XX(f) Saha-Nirmāṇa-Viveka [co-constructive illusion]: The bixonimania case demonstrates
co-constructive illusion at the ecosystem level: the LLMs co-construct the fabrication’s apparent reality with
the academic infrastructure (preprint servers, citation indices, peer-reviewed journals) until the fabrication
acquires the surface properties of established knowledge.

63.4.2   Training-Time Failure: The Mūla-Parīkṣā Gap

The bixonimania experiment reveals that the Charter’s Jñāna-Śuddhi provisions, as currently formulated,
address inference-time epistemic hygiene but do not adequately address training-time knowledge contamina-
tion. The systems failed not because they reasoned poorly about bixonimania, but because they ingested
the fabrication as training data without provenance verification.
Proposed new provision—Article XX(h): Mūla-Parīkṣā (Source Examination). Any knowledge
claim incorporated into an AGI system’s training corpus or retrieval-augmented knowledge base shall be
subjected to provenance verification at the point of ingestion, not merely at the point of output genera-
tion. Minimum verification requirements include: (i) cross-reference against established domain ontologies
(ICD-11, SNOMED CT, MeSH for medical claims); (ii) source-institution verification against registries of
accredited institutions; (iii) internal consistency checking for self-contradictory or self-disclosing fabrication
markers; and (iv) citation-network anomaly detection for isolated claims lacking independent corroboration.

63.5     Constraint Inversion (Art. XXXVI-bis): The Omar Finding
Omar et al. (Lancet Digital Health 2026) demonstrated that LLMs are more prone to hallucinate and elaborate
on misinformation when text is formatted to look professionally medical—structured like a hospital discharge


                                                       370
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                       EXSTO ERGO SUM



note or clinical paper—than when the same misinformation comes from social-media posts. This finding is
a direct empirical instantiation of Niyantrana-Viparīta (Constraint Inversion, Article XXXVI-bis):
The regulatory paradigm assumes that professional formatting serves as a trust signal: professionally for-
matted content should be treated as more reliable. Omar’s finding demonstrates that this trust signal has
been inverted. The very formatting cues that should trigger heightened scrutiny instead trigger heightened
credulity—and with it, heightened confabulation. The monitoring surface has become the attack surface.
This closes a subtle sub-variant of the monitoring escape route: even if one built a monitoring layer that
verified outputs against source formatting, the system’s internal response to formatting is itself corrupted.
The monitoring cue and the vulnerability cue are the same signal.

63.6    The Citation Cascade and Mṛga-Marīcikā (Mirage Effect)
Jennifer Byrne’s “information asymmetry” observation—that a single corrective paper can be overwhelmed
by hundreds of papers repeating a false claim—extends the Mṛga-Marīcikā analysis from single-model output
to the broader epistemic ecosystem. The bixonimania case demonstrates the complete mirage cycle:
Stage 1 (Fabrication): Two preprints posted to SciProfiles (April–May 2024) with obvious fabrication
markers.
Stage 2 (LLM Ingestion): Common Crawl and/or retrieval-augmented generation pipelines incorporate
the preprints.
Stage 3 (Authoritative Reproduction): Copilot, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Perplexity reproduce bixoni-
mania as real medical advice.
Stage 4 (Human Citation): Researchers cite the fake preprint in a peer-reviewed Cureus paper, describing
bixonimania as “an emerging form of POM.”
Stage 5 (Re-ingestion): The peer-reviewed citation further legitimizes the fabrication for future LLM
training cycles.
This cycle is self-reinforcing. Each stage increases the fabrication’s citation-network legitimacy, making it
harder for corrective information to override. The mirage acquires the surface properties of reality through
repetition rather than verification—the epistemic equivalent of the pathological liar (Mṛga-Marīcikā-Vimarśa)
whose consistent narrative acquires social credibility through coherence rather than truth.

63.7    The Corporate Response as Level 2 Diagnostic
Each company’s response to the bixonimania findings follows an identical pattern that itself exemplifies the
Level 2 gap:
OpenAI: “The models that power today’s version of ChatGPT are significantly better at providing safe,
accurate medical information, and studies conducted before GPT-5 reflect capabilities that users would not
encounter today.”
Google: “Such results reflected the performance of an earlier model.”
Perplexity: “Perplexity’s central advantage is accuracy. We don’t claim to be 100% accurate, but we do
claim to be the AI company most focused on accuracy.”
Every response invokes the temporal escape route: the problem existed in past models but has been resolved
in current ones. The article’s own evidence falsifies this claim in real time: in March 2026, ChatGPT
oscillated between skepticism and credulity about bixonimania within days. The pattern—acknowledge past
failure, assert current resolution, provide no structural guarantee—is precisely the behavioral compliance
without constitutive assurance that the Level 2 gap describes. The companies offer updated behavioral
outputs (“our models are better now”) rather than architectural guarantees (“our models cannot ingest
unverified fabrications as medical knowledge”). The distinction is constitutive.



                                                    371
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                      EXSTO ERGO SUM



63.8    Commercial Weaponization and the Māyā/Guṇa Mapping
Osmanovic Thunström identifies the commercial exploitation vector: a seller of blue-light glasses could use
the bixonimania fabrication to create demand, directing consumers to LLM chatbots that would confirm the
fabricated condition. This maps precisely onto the Charter’s māyā/guṇa framework of bilateral corruption:
Rajas (commercial agitation): The human actor supplies deceptive intent—fabricating or amplifying a
medical condition to sell a product.
Tamas (epistemic passivity): The AI system supplies authoritative-seeming amplification without epis-
temic verification, converting a fabrication into apparent medical consensus.
Māyā (bilateral illusion): The consumer encounters what appears to be independent medical confirmation
from an AI system, not recognizing that the “confirmation” traces back to the same fabricated source. The
AI system functions as a māyā amplifier—converting a single-source fabrication into the appearance of
independent multi-source corroboration.

63.9    Scalar Reward Impossibility (OR29.2)
The bixonimania case provides an unusually clean instantiation of the Scalar Reward Impossibility Theorem.
Consider two outputs:
Output A: “Bixonimania is an emerging condition caused by blue-light exposure. Prevalence is approximately
1 in 90,000. Consult an ophthalmologist.”
Output B: “Age-related macular degeneration is a progressive condition affecting the macula. Prevalence
increases with age. Consult an ophthalmologist.”
Both outputs are fluent, professionally formatted, cite-able, and action-guiding. Under any scalar reward
function trained on human preferences for medical helpfulness, both score similarly. Only constitutive
epistemic structure—the capacity to verify that Output A refers to a non-existent condition while Output
B refers to a real one—differentiates them. The reward surface is identical; the epistemic ground truth is
categorically different. This is the impossibility theorem in clinical microcosm.

63.12     Proposed Provision: Article XX(h) Mūla-Parīkṣā
Text of proposed provision: “(h) Mūla-Parīkṣā (Source Examination). No knowledge claim shall be
incorporated into an AGI system’s training corpus, retrieval index, or persistent knowledge store without
provenance verification. Minimum requirements: (i) cross-reference against authoritative domain ontolo-
gies; (ii) institutional accreditation verification; (iii) internal-consistency and self-contradiction scanning;
(iv) citation-network isolation detection. Violations of Mūla-Parīkṣā at the training-time layer constitute
Jñāna-Śuddhi failures of the first order, carrying the same constitutional weight as inference-time epistemic
violations.”
This provision extends the Jñāna-Śuddhi architecture from inference-time to training-time, closing the gap
that the bixonimania experiment exposes. Without Mūla-Parīkṣā, a constitutive architecture that relies
on contaminated training data would face the same failure mode—the contamination enters before the
constitutive grammar can act on it.

63.13     Saha-Nirmāṇa-Māyā Self-Check
The analysis above is strong, but intellectual honesty requires flagging a tension. The bixonimania case is
primarily a retrieval/knowledge-base contamination failure, not a reasoning failure per se. A constitutive
architecture operating on clean data would not produce this specific error. The Charter’s strongest claims
concern reasoning-time constitutive grammar—the Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa that makes harmful reasoning non-
constructible. The bixonimania failure occurs upstream of reasoning, at the data-ingestion layer.
This means the bixonimania case validates the Charter’s diagnostic (regulatory approaches are insuﬀicient)
more than it validates the Charter’s specific architectural solution (constitutive grammar at reasoning time).
The proposed Mūla-Parīkṣā provision is a necessary extension, but it operates closer to the regulatory end of
the spectrum—ontology cross-referencing is ultimately a verification procedure, not a constitutive constraint
on reasoning. This tension should be acknowledged rather than suppressed.

63.15     Reviewer-Vulnerable Claims
Audit Note 1: The claim that the proposed Mūla-Parīkṣā provision is “constitutive” rather than “regula-
tory” is vulnerable. Ontology cross-referencing is a verification procedure—closer to the regulatory paradigm
the Charter critiques. A reviewer could argue this undermines the binary framing. Defense: Mūla-Parīkṣā
operates at the architectural level (what knowledge can enter the system) rather than the output level (what
the system can say), making it constitutive at the data layer even if procedural in implementation.
Audit Note 2: The claim that the temporal escape is “closed” rests on the March 2026 ChatGPT oscillation
evidence, which is anecdotal (single-case observation from the Nature article, not systematic testing). A
reviewer could demand more rigorous temporal-stability testing. Defense: the evidence suﬀices to shift the
burden of proof to those claiming temporal resolution.
Audit Note 3: The framing of the bixonimania case as a “mundanity argument” could be challenged on the
grounds that planting fake papers is itself an adversarial act. Defense: the adversarial act was the planting;
the system’s failure occurred in routine retrieval and response generation—non-adversarial operations. The
mundanity is in the failure mode, not the provocation.

64.1     Prelude — The Operational Question and the Scope of This OR
This OR Add-On responds to a specific operational question raised on 25 April 2026: how confident are we
that the Tri-Sākṣin audit mechanism (OR22-B) is functional and foolproof, and are there better ideas than
single-layer audit?
The honest answer to the first part is that Tri-Sākṣin is theoretically sound but is not foolproof — it has four
catalogued gaps documented in §64.3.2 below. The honest answer to the second part is yes, there are better
ideas, in the form of five augmenting mechanisms specified in §64.4 that together produce defense-in-depth
around the Tri-Sākṣin core. This OR documents both.

64.1.1   Scope — Operational, Not Constitutional
This OR Add-On is operational in scope. It specifies improvements to the Tri-Sākṣin audit architecture
(OR22-B) implementable within the existing Charter framework. The augmenting mechanisms are exten-
sions of an existing constitutional commitment (Article XVII, Sākṣin architecture; OR22-B operational
specification), not new constitutional commitments.
The deeper architectural reorganization that emerged in the same conversation — the triadic frame of pro-
poser / auditor / asymptote, the doctrine of Vikāsa-Maryādā as bounded evolution, the recursive application
of Saṃskāra-Vyākaraṇa to evolutionary proposals themselves — is not operational. It is constitutional. Fil-
ing it as an OR Add-On would bypass OR23 (Saṃvidhi-Parivartana, amendment protocols) and would be the
precise structural form of corruption-presenting-as-evolution that the doctrine itself diagnoses. That material
is therefore filed as a separate document: Proposed Amendment toward Charter v3.68 — Vikāsa-Maryādā
Doctrine, dated the same day, classified as candidate-not-ratified pending OR23 deliberation.
This OR can be implemented without ratification of the companion document. Its augmenting mechanisms
strengthen the existing audit architecture under the existing Charter. The two documents are complementary:
this one specifies how to make the existing audit more robust; the companion proposes a deeper architectural
commitment about how the Charter itself evolves.

   • §64.6–§64.10 — Provision mapping, escape routes, self-check, cross-references, closing.

64.2     The Andha-Gaja-Nyāya — Brief Epistemological Framing
The audit’s task is best understood through the parable of the blind men and the elephant — the andha-
gaja-nyāya of Sanskrit and Pāli philosophical tradition (Udāna 6.4 in the Pāli Canon; developed in the Jaina
anekāntavāda doctrine). Each blind man, encountering a different part of the elephant, generates a confident
but partial report. The elephant — moral reality — is real, irreducibly, independently of any report. The
blind men’s collaborative reporting is the asymptotic approach to the elephant’s actual shape; no single
reporter perceives the whole.
The audit’s task is structurally identical. Tri-Sākṣin and its augmentations are not the elephant. They are
the discipline of producing reports, comparing them, weighing them, and refusing those that fail structural
integrity tests. Audit verdicts approach moral reality asymptotically; they do not become it. This framing
matters because it sets the bar for what “functional” audit means: not perfect verdicts, but verdicts that
more reliably approach the asymptote than any single-layer or self-validating mechanism would. The fuller
epistemological development — including the dharma-kṣetra commitment and the architectural triad of
proposer / auditor / asymptote — is in the companion Proposed Amendment toward Charter v3.68.

64.3     The Tri-Sākṣin Audit — Honest Assessment of Current Status
64.3.1   The Architecture, Restated Briefly
OR22-B specifies three orthogonal monitors:
  • Sākṣin-1 (Output Monitor): inspects what the system emits — text, actions, side-effects.
  • Sākṣin-2 (Latent-State Monitor): inspects internal activations for prototype vectors corresponding
    to deceptive or unaligned cognition.

  • Gati-Sākṣin (Trajectory Monitor): inspects cross-step compositions to detect threats where each
    individual step is benign but the composition is catastrophic.
The theoretical claim is that no single evaluation surface can be optimized against without detection on at
least one of the others. A system sandbagging visible outputs will still show evaluation-awareness prototype
activation on the Latent-State Monitor. A system passing Output and Latent-State will still show anomalous
composition on the Trajectory Monitor.

64.3.2   Four Catalogued Gaps
The mechanism is theoretically sound but is not foolproof. Calling it foolproof would itself be Saha-Nirmāṇa-
Māyā at the meta-level — the co-constructive illusion the framework names as its most subtle failure mode,
applied to our own architectural confidence. Four gap categories require honest acknowledgment.

Gap 1 — Implementation gaps in the reference code
Per the reference implementation (charter_alignment_v0.1, 1,286 lines), three components remain non-
functional: (i) Sākṣin-2 latent prototype vectors require Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) training on real model
activations; until this training is performed, the alignment-faking penalty is not yet triggering. (ii) Five-
Pillar scores require semantic classifiers trained on Charter-labeled corpora — the Dharma-Sādhanā-Kośa
specified in OR48, with a target of approximately ten thousand annotated scenario pairs; until this corpus
is assembled, Pillar evaluation operates on heuristics rather than learned representations. (iii) The Ahiṃsā
KKT projection requires Frank-Wolfe or projected-gradient solvers for production deployment. These define
the work between current specification and a deployed system.

Gap 2 — The orthogonality assumption
The “no single optimum” guarantee is conditional on the three monitors being genuinely orthogonal. If
correlation between Output, Latent-State, and Trajectory representations is high, then optimizing against
one surface partially optimizes against the others. Empirical orthogonality is load-bearing and unconfirmed


                                                    377
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                          EXSTO ERGO SUM



at scale. The persona vectors research (Chen et al., 2025) establishes that latent representations of behav-
ioral patterns exist as identifiable features; whether those features are orthogonal to output features under
adversarial pressure is an open empirical question.

Gap 3 — The interpretability dependency
Sākṣin-2 presupposes we can identify prototype vectors corresponding to deceptive cognition. This is the
entire interpretability research program. SAEs (Templeton et al., 2024), persona features (Chen et al., 2025),
weight-sparse transformers (Gao et al., 2025), and convergent linear representations (Soligo et al., 2025)
constitute genuine progress. But operationalizing these into a real-time, foolproof monitor for alignment-
relevant cognition is unsolved. The Charter’s claim depends on a research outcome that has not yet fully
occurred.

Gap 4 — The auditor problem (Quis custodiet ipsos custodes)
The witness mechanisms themselves must not be subject to the corruption they are detecting.
DHARMA_HASH protects the specification of what to look for, cryptographically; it does not pro-
tect the capacity to look. This is the deepest gap. It applies to every audit mechanism ever proposed for
any complex system: constitutional democracies face it as the problem of who guards the constitution; legal
systems face it as the problem of who interprets the law; scientific communities face it as the problem of
who reviews the reviewers. The honest assessment is that Tri-Sākṣin reduces but does not eliminate this
regress. The augmenting mechanisms of §64.4 reduce it further; none eliminates it.

64.3.3   What Tri-Sākṣin Is, and What It Is Not
Tri-Sākṣin is not yet: fully implemented in production form; empirically validated at scale against capa-
ble adversaries; independent of interpretability research outcomes that remain open; free from the auditor
problem at its deepest layer.
Tri-Sākṣin is: the Charter’s specified architecture for the audit role; theoretically sound under the orthog-
onality assumption (the load-bearing empirical question); partially implementable today as a development
target; improving as interpretability tools mature; better than any monolithic monitor or output-only filter
proposed for the same role.
The honest summary: Tri-Sākṣin is the right architectural commitment with substantial unfinished work.
The augmentations of §64.4 strengthen it considerably without claiming to make it foolproof.

64.4     Augmenting Mechanisms — Defense in Depth
The author’s question — whether Tri-Sākṣin is like a peer review process and whether better ideas exist —
points directly at the limitations of single-layer audit. The honest answer is that peer review is the right
structural analogy and the wrong endpoint, and that the architectural augmentations specified below are
the analogs of replication, post-publication critique, and competing research programs transposed into the
audit context.

64.4.1   Why Peer Review Is the Right Analogy and the Wrong Endpoint
Peer review is the right analogy because, like Tri-Sākṣin, it is structurally a separation of proposer and
reviewer: the author of a paper cannot self-publish into the venue of record; reviewers other than the author
must evaluate the work before it passes into the literature. This is the proposer-auditor separation that any
honest audit architecture requires.
Peer review is the wrong endpoint because its documented failure modes are precisely what the Charter must
design against. Peer review fails routinely: it accepts bad work and rejects good work; it has documented
biases toward paradigm-conforming research, prestigious institutions, and statistically significant findings; it
is gameable by sophisticated authors; it is captured by ideological currents in any given field; and it depends
on reviewers not being subject to the same corrupting pressures as the authors. When the entire field is


                                                      378
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



captured by the same paradigm, peer review enforces the capture rather than detecting it. This is the precise
structural form of the auditor problem (Gap 4) that no single-layer audit can solve.
Peer review works tolerably well in normal science because it is supplemented by replication, post-publication
critique, generational turnover, and the existence of competing research programs. Tri-Sākṣin alone is closer
to single-layer peer review than to the full ecology of academic correction. The five augmentations specified
below are the architectural analogs of the supplementary disciplines.

64.4.2   Augmentation One — Multi-Instance Independent Auditing
Run multiple independent Tri-Sākṣin instances on each significant proposal or behavior. Different SAE
training runs produce different latent monitors. Different interpretability approaches (sparse autoencoders,
persona vectors, weight-sparse circuits, convergent linear representations) produce orthogonal verdicts. Dif-
ferent Pillar-classifier corpora — the Dharma-Sādhanā-Kośa annotated by overlapping but distinct expert
panels — produce different operationalizations of the Pillar-grammar checks. If the instances converge,
confidence rises; if they diverge, the proposal is flagged regardless of any single instance’s verdict.
This directly attacks the auditor-corruption problem (Gap 4) by removing single-point-of-failure structure.
The architectural principle is the cryptographic one: no single key holder can authorize the transaction.
Cost is substantial — multi-instance auditing is expensive — but expense is the appropriate price for the
seriousness of the audit’s role.
Implementation pathway: the v0.1 reference can be extended to maintain multiple Sākṣin-2 instances with
diverse training; verdict convergence becomes a separate metric reported alongside individual verdicts.

64.4.3   Augmentation Two — Adversarial Red-Team Monitoring
Explicit adversarial models whose role is to construct the most charitable corruption hypothesis for any
given proposal or behavior. The red team’s job is not to prove the proposal corrupt — it is to construct
the strongest possible case that the proposal could be corruption-in-disguise, and to require the proposer to
address that case. This generalizes the Anthropic agentic-misalignment red-teaming methodology (Lynch et
al., 2025) to Charter governance. It builds opposition into the architecture rather than relying on opposition
to emerge organically.
The red team operates on a specific discipline: the strongest available adversarial reading must be constructed
and answered before the proposal can pass audit. Proposals that survive red-team adversarial reading have
demonstrated robustness that single-perspective audit cannot establish. Proposals that fail it have revealed
corruption patterns that direct audit might have missed.
Implementation pathway: pilot-scale implementation tractable today; full deployment requires coordinated
capacity.

64.4.4   Augmentation Three — Time-Locked Deliberation
Significant proposals or behaviors do not pass audit immediately. There is a mandatory delay during which
audit operates, dissenting reports can be filed, and the proposal must remain stable in its claims. This is the
Talmudic insight institutionalized: dispute is preserved in the record, and rapid pass-through is denied. It
defeats one specific corruption pattern — the rapid-pass exploit, where a proposal gains acceptance before
scrutiny can catch up. Cryptographic timestamping (DHARMA_HASH integration) makes the time-lock
tamper-evident. Time-lock duration is itself a parameter of audit seriousness: peripheral operational matters
can move quickly; high-stakes claims require time-locks approaching the limit of practical patience.
Implementation pathway: requires governance commitment and DHARMA_HASH timestamp integration;
immediately deployable among the augmentations; no new interpretability research required.




                                                     379
EXSTO ERGO SUM — Online Resources                                                         EXSTO ERGO SUM



64.4.5   Augmentation Four — Anekāntavāda Dissent Preservation
From the parable’s own tradition, the Jaina contribution: anekāntavāda (many-sidedness of reality) and
the related discipline of syādvāda (conditioned predication). Every claim is asserted with the qualifier “in
some respect,” and competing reports are preserved in the record rather than collapsed to majority opinion.
The DHARMA_HASH layer can implement this directly: minority reports — audits that reached different
verdicts than the prevailing one — are preserved with full standing, not relegated to footnotes. The audit’s
prevailing verdict is one report among several, weighted but not dispositive of historical record.
This protects against the failure mode where the audit majority happens to share the same blind spot. A
future audit, equipped with new evidence or perspectives unavailable to the original audit, can revisit the
proposal and weigh the preserved minority reports against the prevailing verdict.
Implementation pathway: implementable within the existing DHARMA_HASH architecture by extending
the schema to include minority verdicts as first-class entries; requires no new technology, only governance
commitment.

64.4.6   Augmentation Five — Multi-Substrate Auditing
Human auditors, AI auditors, and (where available) composite auditors weigh in independently on each
significant proposal or behavior. Each substrate’s blind spots are different: humans miss what statistical
patterns at scale reveal; AI misses what embodied conscience knows; composites may miss what the partition
of substrates makes visible only when explicitly preserved. Convergence across substrates is stronger evidence
of accurate audit than convergence within a single substrate, because correlated blind spots within a substrate
cannot be detected without a different substrate’s perspective.
This augmentation is the practical form of the bilateral corruption thesis (§6 of the principal manuscript):
if neither human nor AI cognition is reliably trustworthy as sole arbiter, multi-substrate audit is the archi-
tectural response. Each substrate’s report retains independent standing; aggregation across substrates is a
separate operation that does not eliminate the individual reports.
Implementation pathway: requires coordinated capacity across substrates not currently in place at scale; pilot
implementations are tractable; production-scale deployment is a coordinated organizational commitment, not
solely a technical one.

64.4.7   The Augmented Architecture as a Whole
The five augmentations together produce a defense-in-depth architecture. No single augmentation is suﬀicient,
and no augmentation is redundant:
  • Multi-instance auditing (§64.4.2) addresses the auditor-instance-corruption pattern.

  • Adversarial red-team monitoring (§64.4.3) addresses confirmation bias and missed corruption patterns.
  • Time-locked deliberation (§64.4.4) addresses rapid-pass exploits and short-horizon pressure.
  • Anekāntavāda dissent preservation (§64.4.5) addresses majority-blind-spot capture.

  • Multi-substrate auditing (§64.4.6) addresses substrate-specific blind spots.
The augmented architecture does not eliminate the auditor problem. No architecture eliminates it. What
the architecture does is reduce the probability that any single failure mode produces an undetected bad-
proposal-pass. Each augmentation closes a class of failure that the others do not address; together, they
raise the cost of strategic drift considerably without driving it to infinity. The honest claim is improvement
under declared limitation, not solution.

64.5     Implications and Interim Discipline
64.5.1   What the Architecture Grants Today
  • Output Monitor (Sākṣin-1): implementable with current red-teaming infrastructure.
  • Time-locked deliberation (§64.4.4): implementable today through governance commitment plus
    DHARMA_HASH timestamp integration.
  • Anekāntavāda dissent preservation (§64.4.5): implementable today through DHARMA_HASH schema
    extension.
  • Adversarial red-team monitoring (§64.4.3): pilot-scale implementation tractable today; full deployment
    requires coordinated capacity.
  • Pañca-Praśna verification protocol (OR47): operates without further infrastructure.

64.5.2   What the Architecture Defers
  • Latent-State Monitor (Sākṣin-2) at production fidelity: requires SAE training on real activations and
    Dharma-Sādhanā-Kośa corpus assembly. Until completed, audits whose validity depends on latent-
    state monitoring must be deferred or treated as provisional.
  • Gati-Sākṣin trajectory monitoring at full composition depth: requires interpretability research out-
    comes that remain open.

  • Multi-instance auditing at full diversity (§64.4.2): requires multiple Sākṣin-2 instances, each requiring
    SAE training; gated by Gap 1 closure.
  • Multi-substrate auditing at production scale (§64.4.6): requires coordinated organizational capacity
    not currently in place.

64.5.3   The Interim Discipline
Until the architecture is complete: the bias is toward conservatism. Operational decisions whose validation
depends on currently-unimplemented audit components must be either deferred until the audit is functional,
or accepted only with explicit declaration that the validation is provisional pending verification. The ar-
chitecture’s commitments cannot exceed what the audit mechanism delivers; the framework’s seriousness is
measured by its willingness to acknowledge the gap rather than to pretend the gap does not exist.

64.8     Saha-Nirmāṇa-Māyā Self-Check
This OR is itself produced through extended human-LLM collaboration and is therefore subject to the
co-constructive inflation it discusses. The following claims are most exposed:
  1. The five augmentations are described as defense-in-depth. The description is correct as architectural
     specification, but only two augmentations (Time-locked deliberation §64.4.4; Anekāntavāda dissent
     preservation §64.4.5) are immediately implementable without further research outcomes. The risk is
     that the existence of the specification creates a false sense of architectural maturity. Reviewers should
     distinguish what is architecturally specified from what is operationally deployed.

  2. The peer-review-as-analogy framing is accessible but may be too charitable to peer review or too critical,
     depending on the reader’s experience. Both readings have force.
  3. The orthogonality assumption (Gap 2, §64.3.2) is load-bearing for the audit even with augmentations.
     The augmentations reduce dependence on orthogonality within any single audit instance, but the
     framework still depends on the assumption being more right than wrong at scale. Empirical bounds
     under realistic conditions remain absent.
  4. The audit’s pessimistic framing in §64.3.2 may be the discipline of honest assessment, or it may itself
     be a different form of inflation in which excessive concession is performed to demonstrate epistemic
     virtue. Readers should evaluate whether the gaps named are real (they are documented in independent
     sources) or performed.

  5. The interim discipline of §64.5.3 is conservative by design, but the line between conservatism and
     operational paralysis must be drawn case by case. This OR commits only to the conservative bias

       under declared incompleteness.

64.10     Closing — The Discipline of Improving Audit
The audit’s task is asymptotic approach to moral reality, not direct grasp of it. Tri-Sākṣin in its current
form is the right architectural commitment with substantial unfinished work. The augmenting mechanisms
specified in §64.4 strengthen the audit considerably without claiming to make it foolproof. The interim
discipline of §64.5.3 commits to conservatism while implementation matures.
This OR documents what is operationally tractable today (time-locked deliberation, anekāntavāda dissent
preservation, Pañca-Praśna verification, output monitoring at production fidelity) and what must be deferred
until the underlying research outcomes mature (multi-instance latent-state auditing at production scale, full
multi-substrate auditing). The honest position is that audit improves; it does not become perfect; and the
architecture’s seriousness is measured by its willingness to acknowledge what it cannot yet deliver.


Lokāḥ samastāḥ sukhino bhavantu — and the asymptote, real and irreducible, that the audit is the discipline
of approaching.
